articles.headline: Giants' J.J. McCarthy returns against Eagles after hip injury sent QB to locker room
keyFacts: New York Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy returned to Sunday's game against the Philadelphia Eagles after being evaluated for a hip injury.
McCarthy suffered the injury in the third quarter following a hard hit from Eagles linebacker Zack Baun.
Jameis Winston temporarily replaced McCarthy and led a touchdown drive before McCarthy returned to the game.
body: The New York Giants appear to have survived another injury scare at the quarterback position. J.J. McCarthy returned to Sunday's game against the Philadelphia Eagles after spending time in the sideline medical tent and locker room while being evaluated for a hip injury.

With McCarthy initially deemed questionable to return, the Giants turned back to Jameis Winston, who started four games before McCarthy replaced him atop the depth chart. Winston led a touchdown drive before he headed back to the sideline.

McCarthy took a hard hit to his lower abdomen on a quarterback keeper in the third quarter. Eagles linebacker Zack Baun led with his helmet while attempting to stop McCarthy's run and made contact with McCarthy's side on the tackle.

McCarthy attempted to throw on the sideline before heading to the locker room and was in obvious pain after he completed his throwing motion. He grabbed at his side and fell to the turf as medical staff came to his assistance. Despite the clear discomfort, he was able to get back into game action just before the end of the quarter.

The Giants were mostly quiet on offense during McCarthy's Week 9 start and scored only six points before he left with the injury. McCarthy was 9-for-13 for 101 passing yards and ran three times for another 11 yards ahead of his brief exit.

Although it seems that McCarthy will remain in action beyond this week, if the injury acts up on him and forces him to miss time, his potential absence may be a significant blow to the NFC East-leading Giants. Already without Jaxson Dart for the rest of the year due to the torn knee ligaments he suffered in Week 2, New York traded for McCarthy as a potential season-long solution. His effectiveness upon insertion into the lineup in the fourth quarter of the Week 6 loss to the New Orleans Saints and in his first start the following week came as a pleasant surprise and gave the Giants reason to believe they could maintain their division lead.

Winston has been serviceable in his own right, so perhaps the Giants could stay afloat if they are ever forced to hand the keys back to him. He went 2-1-1 in his four starts before McCarthy replaced him, and that stretch included a 326-yard performance in the tie with the Washington Commanders and a 250-yard outburst the previous week in a victorious effort. Winston's lack of consistency has long been a limiting factor in his ability to command an offense as a starter, however.

articles.headline: World Of Warcraft: Forever Player Already Hits Level Cap As Users Return To Azeroth In Record Numbers
keyFacts: Player Daniel Gobey reached the maximum level cap in World of Warcraft: Forever in just three days, according to the article.
Blizzard stated that Forever is one of the strongest launches in the history of Warcraft, attracting record player counts.
World of Warcraft VP Holly Longdale reported that the game is seeing the highest number of new players for a launch in 15 years.
body: World of Warcraft: Forever, a throwback version of the massive multiplayer RPG old enough to drink, is giving everyone an opportunity to relive past glories. Turning back the clock to the gameâs first year, with new content and quality of life improvements, the concept worked wonders for RuneScape, and is seemingly doing even better for Blizzard. Forever is one of the strongest launches in Warcraftâs history according to the studio. Among this new wave of players, one familiar face is already up to his old tricks, maxing out the level cap in a matter of days.

Back in 2019, Daniel Gobey, better known as âJokerD,â was the first player to hit the level 60 cap when World of Warcraft Classic launched. As his handle suggests, Gobey is something of a troublemaker, achieving that record by taking advantage of server quirks to juice his rapid ascent. While Blizzard hopes their players will take a more leisurely approach to the latest homecoming, Gobey has once again taken the crown. Reaching the maximum level in Forever in just three days flat. Albeit this time only making use of shorter cooldowns on Undead characters. Upon hitting the milestone, a GM emerged, greeted his party and set off fireworks.
“That was awesome,” said Gobey. “That was not something I was expecting.”

That Gobey remains the record holder in this horde is an even greater feat, given that Forever has collected one of the largest concurrent player counts in the gameâs history. “Another statistic is filling our hearts,” posted World of Warcraft VP Holly Longdale, “we are seeing the most NEW players for a WoW launch in 15 YEARS! Welcome all! Weâre so happy youâre here experiencing Azeroth for the first time alongside those of us playing it for the first time…AGAIN.”

While success stories within Xboxâs convoy are something of a rarity these days, the launch of Forever has gone supremely well. While day one surges usually lead to sweating servers and overcrowding, it seems Blizzard were far more prepared with their infrastructure. And itâs a blessing they did, as 22 years of players seem to be returning to their old spawning grounds.

articles.headline: Broncos DB Devon Key awarded wild interception in the Panthers' end zone after Denver challenge
keyFacts: Broncos defensive back Devon Key intercepted a pass in the end zone during the game against the Carolina Panthers.
Officials initially ruled the play an incomplete pass, but a successful Denver challenge proved the ball never hit the ground.
Following the touchback resulting from the interception, the Broncos executed an 80-yard touchdown drive to take the lead.
body: In Sunday’s matchup between the Carolina Panthers and the Denver Broncos, a dropped touchdown pass turned into an unbelievable interception thanks to a well-timed challenge.

Towards the end of the third quarter, Panthers quarterback Bryce Young threw a pass to tight end Tommy Tremble in the end zone. Though the ball did end up in the hands of Broncos defensive back Devon Key, it looked like it hit the ground first, leading officials to rule the play an incomplete pass.

However, Denver used its challenge flag, leading to a review that proved successful for the Broncos. As Tremble went down while trying to make the catch, the ball rolled off his wrist before bouncing off his hand, with Key in just the right position to pluck it out of the air. It never actually hit the ground at all, leading officials to overturn the call and rule it a Denver pick.

Because the play was ruled dead, Key did not get a chance to make a return, but the Broncos were given a touchback as a result of the call. Quarterback Bo Nix then led the team down the field on a 14-play, 80-yard touchdown drive to take a 19-15 lead.

On 4th and 1 the Lions swing for the fences and give it to their home run hitter Jahmyr Gibbs. I think those analogies make sense … anyway he speeds out wide to the right, finds the edge and races in for the score. That is Gibbs’ 11th touchdown of the season. He only needs two more to over take Terrell Davis on 61 scores in the first four seasons of a career. The Lions running back is something truly special.

Bryce Young is on fire right now. He hits John Metchie on the sideline with a perfectly timed pass then finds Jalen Coker with a quick release as he evades a sack. Just too good from the young quarterback. Carolina are at their own 40-yard line on 2nd down.

Denver are quickly into the 3rd and long and is rocked!!! Patrick Jones delays his pass rush and brings the QB down. This game has turned completely on its head and the crowd are loving it. Bryce Young will be out to extend the lead with 87 yards to travel.
Taylor Swift is enjoying that one. The tight end takes the shovel pass and smashes over for the score on 4th down. Jets need more than field goals now.

Denver keep tabs on Carolina in the red zone and bring up 3rd and 9. Young unleashes a fastball to Darren Waller who races from right to left across the face of the end zone. The big tight end leaps, comes down with it and Carolina have the lead!! The 34-year-old Waller seriously rolling back the years.

Jason Sanders misses a field goal on his fifth try and Mahomes is BACK quickly to help move the Chiefs into field goal range. Harrison Butker misses the boot and gets another go and misses again. Both just wide right. That can’t be good with Justin Tucker waiting to replace him on the practice squad.

WOW! The big tight end goes up high in the left side of the end zone and just comes down in bounds. Incredible catch from Tommy Tremble. Bryce Young cashes in on the Bo Nix interception on 14 play, 86-yard drive. Game on!

Riley Moss has joined Jaylen Waddle in being evaluated for concussions for the Broncos. On 3rd and 9 the Panthers get 8 with a pass to Waller. What are they going to do? They’re gambling. Chuba Hubbard finds the gap to the left and rips off 24 yards!!! What a play! Almost 1st and Goal for Carolina.

articles.headline: Coordinated disturbances haunt grids worldwide. Here’s how researchers solved the mystery.
keyFacts: Researchers discovered that synchronized electrical frequency drops occurring worldwide every 60 seconds are caused by internet-connected batteries checking their charge.
Data center backup power systems in Ireland caused minute-by-minute frequency drops to quadruple between 2016 and 2021, according to grid data.
Researchers recommend that manufacturers add randomization to battery and smart device schedules to prevent potential grid blackouts.
body: For years, mysterious electrical anomalies have been flummoxing grid managers around the world. Every 60 seconds, the frequency on the grid would drop a tiny bit.
Even weirder: The sags happened at the exact same time on power grids across countries and continents.
It was a mystery that Dirk Witthaut, a researcher at Forschungszentrum Jülich in Germany, couldn’t pass up.

Germany’s largest transmission system operator, Tennet Germany, brought the puzzle to Witthaut, and it took years of investigative and modeling work to determine the cause. From Europe to Australia, the U.S. to Malaysia, the same pattern shows up in the data.
Such frequency drops aren’t unheard of, but they are troubling. And the regularity with which they have been occurring can make the phenomenon feel even more ominous.
Balancing the grid

The grid’s orderly operation relies on the frequency being kept within a certain range. If the oscillations get get too large, or if grid operators don’t know the cause and respond improperly, they can lead to blackouts. Even if the sags don’t cause blackouts, they can damage equipment in power plants if they go unchecked, especially in hydropower turbines.

Hydropower plants have historically been a main driver of so-called ultra-low frequency oscillations (UFLOs). Every turbine vibrates, and if those vibrations occur with a certain regularity, known as the resonant frequency, they can magnify, sometimes to dangerous levels. Think of a wine glass breaking before an opera singer’s mighty pipes — that’s resonance.

So Witthaut and his team started investigating hydropower, the most obvious potential culprit. They used a computer model of a hydropower plant control system on the Scandinavian grid to test the hypothesis.

While they managed to find conditions that could generate a resonance that peaked once per minute, they couldn’t explain why it persisted for so long. Typically, resonances in mechanical systems will come and go, and so will the accompanying signal on the electrical grid. But this frequency drop kept happening minute after minute after minute. Every 60 seconds, without fail.
It then dawned on the team that anything operating with such clockwork required, well, a clock. How else could they explain the uncanny timing?
Searching for clues

To that hypothesis, the researchers started close to home, installing more than 80 smart power quality meters around the Jülich campus. The research site is outfitted with medium- and low-voltage distribution lines, transformers, solar panels, and battery energy storage systems that serve as uninterruptible power supplies (UPS). It also has a high-performance computer system as well as the usual office computers powered by much smaller UPS devices. The power quality meters sampled a range of attributes, including frequency, voltage, current, and power, once every three seconds.
Before long, the research team had its answer. The measurements recorded on the transformer attached to the battery energy storage system peaked every minute, just like on the bigger power grids.

It turns out that many stationary batteries, from data center UPSes to large grid-scale batteries, check their state-of-charge every minute. Since these devices are internet-connected, their clocks are in near perfect synchronicity. Every time one checks its charge, the disturbance is imperceptible on the wide grid. But when they all do it together, that disruption becomes apparent.
To find evidence that UPSes were the main culprit on the grid, Witthaut and his team turned to data provided by grid operators. They found their answer in Ireland.

There, data centers have grown to consume a large fraction of the country’s electricity. By 2022, data centers represented 18% of the load on Ireland’s grid, and each facility is served by a fleet of UPSes. Sure enough, between 2016 and 2021, the minute-by-minute frequency drop on the Irish grid quadrupled from 3 milli-Hertz (mHz) in 2016 to 12 mHz in 2021. More recently, some drops have exceeded 20 mHz.

Ireland’s 50 Hz grid is built to withstand swings of plus or minus 200 mHz, though the grid operator would rather limit the swings to 100 mHz. In that range, 20 mHz isn’t a lot, but data centers aren’t the only loads on the grid. If other loads also cause the frequency to sag, the extra bump from every UPS checking its state-of-charge could push the grid toward blackout conditions.
The solution

The problem is entirely preventable. Rather than check state-of-charge exactly on the minute, Witthaus and team recommend that UPS and grid-scale battery manufacturers add some randomization to the schedule.

While UPSes are driving the problem today, there’s a risk that the phenomenon could persist. The researchers also tested IoT devices. In devices as diverse as a smart oven and Raspberry Pi clusters, they were able to detect periodic power fluctuations. The fix is also a simple software patch, but many IoT devices go unpatched. A recent study found that less than 3% of IoT devices are running the latest firmware.

Regulators may soon have to step in to demand changes, but they can only address their corner of the grid. Given the global nature of the issue, it’ll ultimately require global coordination. The mystery may be solved, but the problem could remain for years to come.

articles.headline: Why your laptop fans spin up without any warning
keyFacts: Sudden laptop fan noise is often caused by restricted airflow from dust or intensive background activity.
Users can clean vents using compressed air and check active resource usage through Task Manager or Activity Monitor.
Checking warranty terms before dismantling the laptop for advanced cleaning is recommended.
body: Why your laptop fans spin up without any warning
With a bit of cleaning and system management, you can keep your laptop fan from jump-scaring you.

You're sitting down with your laptop in front of you, getting a bit of light work done, when suddenly you hear what sounds like a jet engine going off. Your computer's fans start roaring and whirring, but after a short moment, everything is quiet again. If you've ever had your laptop fan sound off without warning like this, there are a few possible causes.

Over the years, laptops have become much better at managing performance and cooling, but even the best laptops of today need strong fans to keep their high-powered components cool in such a compact space. While some fan noise is perfectly normal, persistent or unusually loud bursts can indicate that your laptop is working harder than it needs to. Sudden spikes in fan noise are often caused by intensive background activity or dust restricting airflow. Both are relatively easy to investigate, and there are a few simple ways to check what's making your laptop work harder and address the problem.
How to check and clean your laptop fan

The first thing to check if your laptop fan starts acting up is whether it's getting enough airflow. Make sure you're using it on a hard, flat surface like a table or desk rather than a bed, sofa, or other soft surface that could block its vents. If the fan continues to run loudly, dust buildup around the fans or air vents could be the issue.

Luckily, you can typically clean your fans and air vents without taking the machine apart. First, turn off your laptop, unplug any attached devices, and wait for it to cool. Then locate the air vents, which may be on the underside or sides of the device, depending on the model. Use short bursts of compressed air to dislodge dust and debris, following the instructions on the can. You can then wipe away any loose debris with a clean microfiber cloth.

If this approach doesn't do the trick, you may need to dismantle your laptop for greater access to the fans. Along with compressed air, you can also use an ESD-safe brush to remove dust from the components. This process may be a little advanced for some users, and the exact method depends on the type of laptop you're working with. If you're not comfortable taking apart your laptop yourself, it's worth getting in touch with a technician. Also, before dismantling the machine, check your warranty terms and manufacturer's guidance on user repairs, as opening the laptop or carrying out repairs yourself may affect your coverage.
How to check for intensive background activity

If your laptop's fans continue to get extra loud at random intervals, it's possible the CPU is getting a covert workout. On Windows, tap Ctrl+Shift+Esc to open Task Manager and select Processes to see what's running. Click the CPU column to sort processes by how much processing power they're using, putting the biggest resource hogs at the top. Then, head to Startup apps and disable any programs you don't want launching automatically when you start your laptop. If you're a Mac user, open Activity Monitor (hit Command+Spacebar to open Spotlight Search if you're struggling to find it) and head to CPU to identify the processes using the most resources. Click the % CPU column to sort them, then select a process and click the Stop button, then choose Quit.

Before you get trigger-happy, look out for background processes you can live without instead of quitting them willy-nilly (as doing so can lead to some big crashes). On Windows, if you're not using programs like Calculator, Gaming Services, News and Interests, Phone Link, CTF Loader or Groove Music, you can generally end their processes. On Mac, you can quit lingering processes associated with apps you've already closed, Rosetta applications you're no longer using and disk image processes that are preventing a disk from ejecting. You can also disable Spotlight indexing if you don't need your Mac to maintain a fully indexed library.

articles.headline: Derby game called off just an hour before kick-off as fans block team bus
keyFacts: A Dutch second division match between Vitesse Arnhem and De Graafschap was called off because De Graafschap fans blocked their own team bus.
De Graafschap supporters chained stadium gates shut in protest of away fan restrictions and safety conditions imposed after past trouble.
The Dutch FA stated the situation is unacceptable, referred the matter to disciplinary bodies, and will announce a new match date later.
body: A Dutch second division match had to be called off due to the away team stopping their own bus from reaching the ground.
Rivals Vitesse Arnhem and De Graafschap were due to face-off on Sunday, but the match was abandoned for a bizarre reason.
It is very rare that you see a team’s own fans do anything they can to stop a game taking place Shutterstock editorial
A large number of De Graafschap fans turned up at the club’s stadium and chained the gates shut.
This prevented the players from leaving in the team bus until it was decided that the match would be called off and pushed back to another date.
Vitesse provided official updates throughout before they confirmed it was off and technical director Willem van der Linden released a statement.
He said: “In the lead-up to the match, Vitesse did everything possible, in close cooperation with all parties involved, to still get the match started. Unfortunately, this proved to be unfeasible.

“We deeply regret the situation. Thousands of supporters, partners, Business Club members, and volunteers were already present in the GelreDome. We want to thank everyone for their attendance, patience, and unconditional support.”
It is such an unusual situation that the Mayor of Arnhem Ahmed Marcouch also released a statement.

He said: “Football belongs to everyone. But hospitality is not a licence to disregard safety agreements. Over the past few weeks, we have given De Graafschap every opportunity, ample time and every means to ensure this match could take place safely with away fans present.

“Another attempt was made on Saturday to reach workable agreements. But if supporters say in advance that they do not want to abide by the conditions and their own club cannot guarantee that the agreements will be observed, then that is the end of it.”
Why did the fans block the team bus?
The Kleine Gelderse Derby is a heated affair. Last year, the away fans saw their allocation cut down to just 500.
This didn’t go down well with the supporters, who also had to have banners pre-approved.
The supporters had been banned from attending the game due to trouble in the past Shutterstock Editorial
Their pushback led to the relevant authorities deciding to ban them from attending altogether.
And the fans decided that rather than not being allowed to attend, they’d just stop the game happening instead.
This hasn’t gone down well with the Dutch FA, who have released a statement.
It read: “It is unacceptable that the Vitesse – De Graafschap match cannot go ahead in this way.
“Supporters making football impossible is completely unacceptable. In doing so, they are harming their club, their team, the sport and the thousands of supporters who do come to support football.
“The match will definitely not be played today. In accordance with the regulations, the matter will now be referred to the disciplinary bodies.
“The league board will discuss the exceptional situation further tomorrow.
“More information about the new match date and the consequences will be announced after that.”

articles.headline: All endings in Queen’s Domain and how to unlock them
keyFacts: Queen’s Domain features four different endings that are determined by player decisions at crucial junctures.
Ending one requires completing quests and using the ordinary weapon route, while ending two requires completing Endu's evolution and the Akunra route.
Ending three involves the Okbujo route, and ending four requires finding 69 Silver Skulls after finishing Petrified Garden and repeating previous steps.
body: Queen’s Domain is not an easy game by any means, and your decision-making will determine the ending you unlock. Yes, there are multiple ones (four, to be precise), and the ending depends on certain crucial junctures and the ensuing decision.
Let’s find out the requirements to unlock all the four endings.

Ending two

How to unlock all endings in Queen’s Domain
If you want to unlock all the endings, you should look for the crucial junctures in the following sections. Create a backup so that you can reload and try out a different ending.
Ending one

This is the least complicated ending to reach in the game. You have to complete the quests and take the ordinary weapon route to finish the game. The ending is actually boring, but it’s easy, and takes the least effort.
Ending two

To reach this ending, wait until you complete Endu’s evolution by meeting the movement requirements. Then, you’ll need to get the lens/ideal setup. Once done, you’ll now have to take the Akunra route to finish the story.
Ending three
To get this ending, you’ll have to pursue the Okbujo route once you complete its late-game quests. This is a relatively hard route, so you’ll need to put in some extra efforts.
Ending Four

This is the hardest ending, and for a good reason. Once you finish Petrified Garden, you’ll need to first find 69 Silver Skulls. These skulls can be found in different locations, so it’s not an easy job. Once done, you’ll need to repeat all the steps that you do for the previous ending (Ending three).

articles.headline: Nvidia is investigating Jensen Huang’s relationship with a Chinese spy
keyFacts: Nvidia's board is investigating CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang after reports of a foreign intelligence effort.
US officials believe Alice Huang fed information to Beijing, and Megaspeed is being investigated for allegedly smuggling Nvidia AI chips to China.
The board stated it has no reason to believe national security or secrets were compromised, and Jensen Huang is fully cooperating.
body: Nvidia has announced that it is opening an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who was reportedly recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on the company. A statement posted by the board of directors reads:
Nvidia is investigating Jensen Huang’s relationship with a Chinese spy
Following reports that Nvidia’s CEO had a ‘close relationship’ with an AI exec the company is opening an investigation.

The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation.

The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders. While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information. Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.
The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.

The New York Times reported last month that Huang had developed a “close relationship” with the Megaspeed executive, which he later admitted was romantic in nature in a memo to the company. US officials believe she was feeding information directly back to Beijing.

Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia and is the subject of a Commerce Department investigation into whether it was smuggling AI chips to China. The company’s AI chips are viewed as crucial to the US maintaining technological supremacy. Both the Biden and Trump administrations have restricted their sale to China. President Trump has loosened those restrictions but still bars sales of Nvidia’s most powerful chips to Chinese firms, and the Commerce Department must approve individual firms to handle the chips.

Just as importantly, Jensen Huang has gotten quite cozy with Donald Trump, and there is concern about what insights into the administration’s deliberations around AI he may have been privy to. And whether any of that information may have been shared with Alice Huang, and eventually found its way to Beijing.

articles.headline: Collision between two trains in Egypt kills seven and injures more than 100
keyFacts: Seven people were killed and over 100 injured when two trains collided south of Cairo, the Chief Prosecutor's office said.
Officials said a moving train crashed into a stationary train on the same track, with a conductor among those killed.
President Abdel-Fattah el Sissi ordered an investigation into the crash, while emergency teams worked to clear the wreckage.
body: CAIRO (AP) — Seven people were killed and over 100 others injured when two trains collided Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, the Chief Prosecutor’s office said in a statement. It also said the train’s conductor was among those killed.

The crash occurred in al Ayyat district in Giza province, about 32 miles south of Cairo, when a train traveling to the southwestern Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the Transportation Ministry.

The Chief Prosecutor’s office said late Sunday its investigators had arrived at the site. An inspection indicated that the crash took place when the Giza-Fayyoum train collided with the last carriage of the Cairo-Aswan train, that was stationary on the same track and traveling in the same direction, officials said.

Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years, the government announced modernization initiatives to improve its railways.
People gather at the site where a passenger train derailed in Al-Ayyat, Giza, Egypt, on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. (AP Photo)
Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al Ayyat where the crash occurred, said people living nearby rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances.

Gamal said that he saw around 80 of the injured were taken by ambulances to nearby hospitals. Some passengers were trapped inside one of the carriages of the stationary train and were dead when they were pulled out, he said.
President Abdel-Fattah el Sissi said in a social media post that he ordered a prompt investigation into the crash.
Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian Railway Authority said.
RUSSIA TARGETS EMERGENCY CREWS AT THE SITE OF A DEADLY STRIKE IN SOUTHERN UKRAINE
Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district.
Egypt’s deadliest train crash was in 2002, when more than 300 people were killed after a fire broke out on an overnight train journeying from Cairo to southern Egypt.

articles.headline: Former PlayStation Boss Says Sony Doesn't Need a 'PS6 for $1,200,' It Needs a 'PS5 for $300'
keyFacts: Former PlayStation boss Shawn Layden said Sony should focus on making a cheaper PlayStation 5 rather than an expensive PlayStation 6.
Sony has increased console prices in recent years, citing global economic pressures while console sales suffer.
Sony stated in May that it was still deciding when its next console should launch, amid reports of a possible 2028 or 2029 release.
body: Former PlayStation boss Shawn Layden said he thinks innovation at Sony shouldn't come "from making a PS6 for $1,200" but from making "another PS5 for $300."

As tech costs skyrocket and rumors of pricey gaming consoles swirl, the former president and CEO of Sony Interactive Entertainment America took the time during an appearance on The Trophy Room podcast to encourage the PlayStation maker to consider an unexpected, cheaper course of action. Pointing out how previous hardware leaps have typically offered clearly identifiable innovative qualities from generation to generation, he touched on why the PlayStation 6 simply leaning on "more ray tracing and more teraflops" might not be the best idea.
As Layden put it, "I think we have enough power in the machine."

"The innovation needs to come not from making PS6 for $1,200. It's to make another PS5 for $300," he added. "Now, that would be true innovation. This is the first platform that I've seen that has gone up in price over time. I mean, PS2, at the end of the PS2 era, it was $99. You could buy a PS2 for $99."

The PS5 launched almost exactly six years ago with two primary options for players to choose from: a base version with a disc drive for $499, and a Digital Edition for $399. What seemed like relatively fair price points in 2020 now seems almost like a steal thanks to a series of price increases in recent years. Today, buying a base PS5 directly from PlayStation costs $649, a Digital Edition costs $599, and a Pro costs an unbelievable $899 (up $200 from its reveal price ). Things get even worse when you look at retailers like GameStop .

Sony has put the blame on "continued pressures in the global economic landscape ," but that's done little to lessen the sting for the average buyer. As console sales for Sony, Microsoft , and Nintendo suffer, Layden is of the mind that Sony shouldn't be looking for a way to get to a likely more expensive future but instead a cheaper past.
"I think if I were in their shoes, that's what I'd be doing. I'd be trying to find a way to get the cost down on the 5," he added.

Later, he continued: "It's a hard place to be right now, I think. What the company needs to do is do what it's never done, which is, don't iterate the console. Make it smaller, make it cheaper, do all the things you can around that, but the silicon's fine, the OS is fine. It's more than enough power to build the kind of games all of us want to play."

If you look at the raw console release timeline, we're just about due for the next PlayStation, but many players say they don't want to see a PS6 announced until hardware prices come down. In May, Sony said it was still trying to decide when its next console should launch . It followed a February report that stated the company was considering pushing the device to 2028 – or even 2029 – following previous 2027 launch expectations.

For now, however, we know distressingly little about the PS6. As PlayStation continues battling the backlash against its decision to kill physical discs , one leaker has said RAM and storage for the console alone could cost as much as $680 . Meanwhile, an October patent suggested Sony may be looking into taking advantage of its own take on frame generation . How much the PS6 will cost when all is said and done is a mystery, but the future isn't looking particularly bright .

articles.headline: This is the cheapest RTX 5090 PC we could find — and why we'd pick it over a similarly-powered laptop
keyFacts: CyberPowerPC offers a desktop computer equipped with an Nvidia RTX 5090 graphics card for $7,609.50 after a promotional discount.
The desktop price is lower than the standalone ASUS RTX 5090 graphics card listed on Amazon for $7,679.80.
Desktop RTX 5090 graphics cards deliver higher performance than mobile versions found in laptops due to cooling and power limitations.
body: - The complete desktop costs $70 less than Amazon's listed ASUS graphics card
- CyberPowerPC bundles a desktop RTX 5090 with 32GB DDR5 memory
- Mobile RTX 5090 laptops sacrifice performance compared with desktop graphics cards
Nvidia's GeForce RTX 5090 has become ridiculously expensive, with standalone graphics cards selling for several times their original launch prices.
That makes finding a complete desktop computer equipped with the flagship graphics processor for less than $8,000 particularly interesting.
One configuration currently available from CyberPowerPC costs $7,609.50 after applying a $400.50 promotional discount.
As RTX 5090 scarcity pushes prices higher, this ASUS TUF model costs $7,679.80, offering 32GB GDDR7, PCIe 5.0, HDMI 2.1b, DisplayPort 2.1b, and Axial-tech cooling.
A complete RTX 5090 desktop PC
The GeForce Extreme Creator Gaming PC comes equipped with ASUS's TUF Gaming GeForce RTX 5090, featuring 32GB of GDDR7 memory.
Interestingly, the ASUS TUF Gaming GeForce RTX 5090 is listed on Amazon for $7,679.80; buyers are basically getting the PC at no cost.
The system uses Intel's Core Ultra 5 250KF processor, featuring six performance cores and twelve efficiency cores, alongside a maximum turbo frequency of 5.3GHz.
Although this is not Intel's most expensive desktop processor, its specifications provide a capable foundation for demanding gaming and computing workloads.
The graphics card receives power from a 1,300W fully modular supply, while an Asetek 570LC liquid cooler handles processor temperatures.
The device also includes 32GB of DDR5 memory operating at 6,000MHz, providing sufficient capacity for many demanding applications and modern games.
Storage comes from a 500GB Kingston NVMe solid-state drive using PCIe Gen4 connectivity, although buyers might eventually want additional capacity.
The remaining configuration includes an ASRock Z890-C D5 motherboard, Wi-Fi 7 connectivity, Windows 11 Home and a CyberPowerPC Onyxia II enclosure.
There is also a two-year parts warranty, alongside complimentary service coverage that includes labour and lifetime technical assistance.
Importantly, the advertised $7,609.50 price excludes a monitor, keyboard and mouse, meaning buyers should account for additional peripheral expenses.
RTX 5090 laptops are cheaper, but there is an important difference
One reason this desktop configuration deserves attention is the substantial difference between desktop and laptop versions of Nvidia's flagship graphics processor.
Although gaming laptops advertised with RTX 5090 graphics can cost considerably less, their mobile graphics processors are not equivalent to desktop versions.
Laptop manufacturers must accommodate restricted cooling capacity, battery consumption and physical dimensions, requiring substantially different power configurations.
Consequently, a mobile RTX 5090 generally delivers considerably less graphics performance than its desktop counterpart, despite sharing the same product designation.
The desktop RTX 5090 also provides 32GB of GDDR7 memory, giving it considerable advantages for demanding graphics workloads and local artificial intelligence applications.
This distinction matters because comparing prices without considering the underlying hardware can create misleading impressions about what buyers actually receive.
At $7,609.50, the CyberPowerPC configuration is certainly expensive, although its inclusion of Nvidia's flagship desktop graphics card changes the calculation.
With standalone RTX 5090 cards commanding extraordinary prices, this is practically a case of buying the graphics card and getting the rest of the computer free.

articles.headline: Iran downplays new U.S. task force aimed at disrupting land routes
keyFacts: Iran's military dismissed U.S. Central Command's new Task Force Iron Gate, aimed at disrupting Iranian trade routes, as wordplay.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said indirect negotiations with the U.S. halted due to shock from U.S. midterm election results.
President Trump said resuming U.S. attacks on Iran is highly unlikely if negotiations with Tehran make progress.
body: What to know about the Iran war today:

- Central Command also announced the creation of Task Force Iron Gate, which is supposed to extend the success of the naval blockade to overland routes of trade. The group will be tasked with preventing military technology and illegal revenue streams from entering or exiting Iranian borders, including via the Caspian Sea, but it was unclear if any military force would be brought to bear. Iran's military on Sunday dismissed the new task force as "word play."

- The U.S. military's Central Command announced Friday it is offering up to $20 million and possible relocation in exchange for information about Iran's nuclear program, its facilities, equipment or personnel.
- President Trump confirmed on Friday the U.S. carried out "minor strikes" on Iran, after local state media reported missiles striking Qeshm island in the Strait of Hormuz
Iranian foreign minister says negotiations halted after U.S. midterm elections
Iran's top diplomat said mediators working to broker a deal between the U.S. and Iran haven't traveled since America's midterm elections last week, citing "the shock" of the election results.

"For the past few days, there has been no more travel [by mediators], and the reason for this is the shock that the election results in the United States have caused to everyone," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday on Iranian state television.

"We now have to see how long it will take for them to digest these results, in order to determine how we are going to move forward," Araghchi added, in reference to the Republican Party's heavy losses.
Calling for patience, he said it would "take some time before the atmosphere is favorable for the resumption of mediator travel."

Various regional powers, including Qatar and Pakistan, have been trying for months without success to bring a definitive halt to the war launched by the U.S. and Israel against Iran in late February. Although outright fighting has largely subsided, Iran has continued its efforts to blockade the vital Strait of Hormuz, while the U.S. has maintained a counterblockade of Iranian ports.
CBS/AFP
Trump says U.S. resuming attacks against Iran is "highly unlikely" if talks progress

President Trump said Sunday that resuming attacks on Iran was "highly unlikely," telling CNN in an interview that he believed it wouldn't be necessary to order the U.S. to return to fighting if negotiations with Tehran progress.

Washington and Tehran for weeks have been engaged in indirect, mediated negotiations to end the conflict that has drawn on since February. But talks have stalled as the two sides failed to reach agreements on key issues, like reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's nuclear capabilities. Both have put forward proposals with different sets of conditions in attempts to strike a deal.
Mr. Trump told CNN's Jim Sciutto that resuming an all-out war against Iran "depends on whether or not [Iranian leaders] sign a very strong agreement.

"The answer is highly unlikely it's going to be necessary," the president said. "They're a failing nation. It just came out, you saw this year, 301% inflation. Highly unlikely it will be necessary. I would if necessary, but we hit them really hard. I hit them so hard. You don't know how hard I hit them."
Mr. Trump will speak with 60 Minutes in his first sit-down interview since last week's midterm elections Sunday night at 7 p.m. ET/PT on CBS.
UAE says it rescued 22 crew members from cargo ship fire in Sea of Oman

The United Arab Emirates National Guard said it rescued 22 crew members from a cargo ship that caught fire in the Sea of Oman, without specifying what caused the fire or identifying the vessel. The crew members were all of Arab nationalities, the National Guard said.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center, or UKMTO, a British military organization that monitors maritime security incidents, said Sunday that a tanker caught fire on Saturday about 8 nautical miles northwest of Khasab, Oman, prompting the evacuation of its crew. It was unclear whether it was the same ship whose crew the UAE had helped evacuate.

On Saturday, U.S. forces disabled a St. Kitts-flagged cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman, saying it had attempted to breach the U.S. naval blockade of Iran. Separately, the Iranian military said late Saturday that two tankers had struck mines in the area of the Strait of Hormuz. It did not identify the vessels' flags or destinations.
CBS/AP
Iranian foreign minister says it's "time for the White House" to make a choice in negotiations
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that it's "time for the White House to make its own [choice]" about how to proceed as negotiations to end the war stretch on into a fifth week.
"American voters have made their choice. Time for the White House to make its own," Araghchi said in a social media post.

"Our 2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results," the post continued. "Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell."

Araghchi previously said that, during mediated, indirect talks with the U.S., Iran had presented a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the U.S. agreed to certain conditions.
Houthis claim attack on Riyadh financial district damaged Aramco skyscraper

Yemen's Houthis on Sunday claimed responsibility for an attack on the financial district of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital city, which witnesses said caused damage to a skyscraper belonging to oil giant Aramco. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis had said earlier Sunday that its air defenses intercepted two ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles targeting Riyadh and other regions.

In a statement, Houthi military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the Iran-backed group carried out four military operations using ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones. Saree said the Riyadh airport was targeted in addition to the financial center, Aramco oil storage tanks, and the eastern Saudi city of Abqaiq.

He said the Houthis were responding to attacks in recent days on a village near Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and at a market in southwestern Yemen, which he said left dozens dead or wounded and blamed on Saudi Arabia.
Aramco facilities and infrastructure have been repeatedly struck by the Houthis in recent months, with tankers, refineries, storage areas and the company headquarters all targeted by the group.
"Aramco tower in KAFD has been targeted, that's the sure thing," one witness told AFP, referring to the King Abdullah Financial District. Two other witnesses confirmed seeing damage to the building.
One witness in the area of the Aramco skyscraper told AFP they saw a projectile strike the building but they were unsure what type of projectile it was.
The Saudi Energy Ministry said there were no casualties at the Aramco facility.
AP/AFP
Israel's defense minister says Iran mission "not complete"
Israel's defense minister hinted at a resuming attacks on Iran on Sunday, saying the "mission is not complete."

"With regard to Iran, the mission is still not complete. Iran is trying to renew its efforts to obtain nuclear weapons -- alongside other grave efforts that place the State of Israel in real danger," Israel Katz said.
He also warned the Iran-backed Hezbollah group in Lebanon to not join Tehran in retaliating against Israel.

"We will not withdraw from the security zones in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, and if the terrorist organisation Hezbollah chooses to join Iran in an attack on Israel, it will suffer extremely severe blows," Katz said.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose political bloc failed to reach a majority in the country's elections, has previously suggested he wants to resume attacks on Iran.
However, on the eve of the midterm elections President Trump told the Financial Times newspaper he had no plans to strike Iran.
CBS/AFP
Saudi oil giant's building damaged by intercepted rocket, authorities say

Witnesses in the Saudi capital of Riyadh said they heard a loud explosion Sunday morning and described damage across multiple floors of an Aramco building in the King Abdullah Financial District Some floors appeared to be heavily damaged.
The witnesses spoke on condition of anonymity because of security concerns.

The Saudi-led coalition said its air defenses intercepted two ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles targeting Riyadh and other regions early Sunday, accusing the Houthis of launching the weapons.
The Saudi Energy Ministry said the attempted attack resulted in "falling shrapnel that caused minor damage to the building." It added that there were no casualties.
CBS/AP
Iran's military dismisses new U.S. plan aimed at curbing ground shipping
Iran's military has dismissed the U.S.'s new task force which aims to disrupt Iranian ground shipping routes as "wordplay."
In a statement to Iran's semi-official Fars news agency, a Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesman said Tehran had made preparations and communicates closely with neighbours.

"The Iron Gate plan is merely a wordplay, the Americans cannot achieve their objectives of imposing severe economic pressure to cause economic collapse in Iran through this approach," Mohebbi told the semi-official Fars news agency.
CBS/AFP
Dozens killed in Saudi strikes in Houthi-held region in Yemen, Houthis say
Houthi authorities said Sunday that Saudi strikes killed 33 people, many of them women and children, in Yemen's Sanaa province, as deaths mount in the country's revived civil war.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed in the impoverished country.

The death toll from the Saudi-led coalition's strikes on Al-Shariya village located east of Yemen's capital Sanaa has risen to 33, with 39 people wounded, Houthi health ministry spokesman Anees Alasbahi said in a post on X.
The Houthis' Saba news agency said on Saturday that operations to recover victims from the rubble were ongoing and that "aircraft targeted paramedics with two strikes."
"According to the near-final figures, the dead include 12 men, 8 women and 13 children, while the injured include 16 men, 10 women and 13 children," Alasbahi said.

Saudi Arabia, fighting in Yemen in support of the internationally-recognized government, has not commented on the report. The Saudi-led coalition in a statement on Saturday said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi missile launched towards Riyadh province.
The Iran-backed Houthis, meanwhile, said they had launched multiple missile and drone attacks against Saudi troops and infrastructure both in the Gulf kingdom and Yemen.
Yemen slipped back into war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government in July after years of relative calm, opening a new front in the conflict in the Middle East.
Since then, Saudi Arabia has regularly bombed Houthi positions, while the group has expanded its attacks against the oil-rich kingdom.
U.S. forces disabled commercial vessel in Gulf of Oman, CENTCOM says

U.S. forces disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman on Saturday after the ship's civilian crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to violate the naval blockade against Iran multiple times, U.S. Central Command said.

A U.S. military aircraft fired precision munitions at the stern of St.Kitts-flagged M/V Huda, which disabled the ship after the crew was directed to abandon targeted spaces. The cargo vessel tried to depart regional waters after visiting an Iranian port, CENTCOM said.
"All mariners transiting near Iranian coastal areas or surrounding waters are advised to heed blockade warnings from U.S. forces," CENTCOM said.
Earlier Saturday, CENTCOM said "strict enforcement" of the U.S. blockade on Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz continues.

Iran established a chokehold on the strait, a vital strategic waterway in global trade, at the beginning of the war, and has claimed attacks on tankers. The U.S. says its blockade had redirected 144 commercial vessels through the end of October.
-CBS/AP
U.S. launches new task force to disrupt Iranian ground shipping routes

In what the U.S. military is calling an expansion of the naval blockade, U.S. Central Command announced a new task force Saturday aimed at disrupting the illegal shipment of prohibited items like military technology or illegal revenue streams over ground transportation routes.

"The establishment of Task Force Iron Gate reinforces the success of our ironclad blockade against Iran at sea," U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper said in a statement. "Strengthening CENTCOM's collaboration with U.S. interagency partners will further constrain Iran's ability to finance terrorism, rebuild weapons factories, and replenish their military."

The U.S. said the task force will be made up of about 20 civilian and military personnel, based in Florida, and will be tasked with the goal of "preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue streams across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea."
The announcement made no mention of how the task force would be carrying out its goal, including whether any military operations will be involved.

China, Iran's largest trade partner, has taken to conducting commerce over land, especially by train across central Asia due to the blockade on Iranian ports. The U.S. said the blockade has prevented some $25 billion in Iranian crude oil from being sold, much of it in Asia.

In addition to China, Iran has conducted large amounts of trade over land and via the Caspian Sea with Russia. The landlocked Caspian Sea has proven especially advantageous with a direct route between southwest Russia and northern Iran. Tehran is located just 80 miles south of the Caspian Sea.
Whether any U.S. ships could take to the Caspian Sea was again unclear. CBS News has reached out to the White House for more details.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard lifts self-imposed missile-range limit

Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it has lifted a self-proclaimed limit of 1,200 miles on the range of its ballistic missiles, suggesting the country may seek to develop missiles capable of reaching more distant targets amid fears of renewed all-out war.

The comments by the spokesman of Iran's paramilitary Revolutionary Guard came days after the country's supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khomeini, warned "any kind and level of threat" from the U.S. or Israel would face a response without geographic limits.
Asked at a Tehran press conference about the limit on missile ranges, Gen. Hossein Mohebbi said, "That restriction has been lifted for us."
He did not say whether Iran had missiles capable of exceeding the limit, saying only Iran would "demonstrate these capabilities in practice" rather than make statements.

Iran is not known to have missiles that can go beyond the 1,200-mile limit — a range that puts parts of Greece and the Balkans, the entire Arabian Peninsula, the Levant and most of Egypt within reach. However, U.S. officials have said technology from Iran's space program can be repurposed to build intercontinental ballistic missiles.

The Iranian military, meanwhile, said a tanker east of the Strait of Hormuz had hit a naval mine and caught fire. It did not identify the nationality or destination of the tanker, which it said had turned off its navigational beacon and was sailing in a "prohibited area."
22 killed in Saudi strikes on Yemen's Sanaa province, Houthis say
Saudi strikes killed 22 people, most of them women and children, in Yemen's Sanaa province, as deaths mount in the country's civil war, Houthi media said on Saturday.
More than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed in the impoverished country, according to the U.N.

"The number of victims of the Saudi enemy warplane massacre in the Al-Shariyah area ... has risen to 22 citizens, most of them children and women, while the number of wounded has risen to 30," the Houthis' Saba news agency said.
The Iran-backed group's Al-Masirah TV provided the same toll.
Saba said earlier Saturday that operations to recover victims from the rubble were ongoing and that "aircraft targeted paramedics with two strikes."
The Saudi-led coalition in a statement on Saturday said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi missile launched toward Riyadh province.

On Friday, an attack on a market in Taiz province killed 30 people. The Houthis said Saudi airstrikes were to blame, while Yemen's government forces accused the Iran-backed group of having fired a ballistic missile at the site.
AFP/CBS
Iranian army says forces learned from war with the U.S.
Iran's military is "stronger" and more motivated than it was when the United States and Israel started the war in February, Iranian state media reported on Saturday, citing an army spokesman.

"Today, the Islamic Republic's armed forces... having gained experience from direct confrontation with the United States and the Israeli regime, are on higher alert and are stronger than they were at the beginning of the war," spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said, according to the state news agency IRNA.
"They now possess greater motivation, commitment, and self-confidence."
CBS/AFP
Trump confirms U.S. carried out more "minor strikes" on Iran
President Trump confirmed on Friday the U.S. carried out "minor strikes" in Iran, after local state media reported missiles striking Qeshm Island on the Strait of Hormuz.
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Mr. Trump was asked whether the U.S. carried out more strikes on the island.
"I don't want to talk about it," the president said. "We do minor strikes. They built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe 5."

On Saturday, Iran's Tasnim news agency reported that two missiles had struck Qeshm island, added that there was no official information on the damage. Iranian state television also reported two explosions on the island.
White House offers up to $20 million reward for information on Iran's nuclear program
The Trump administration is offering a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran's nuclear program, the U.S. military's Central Command announced Friday.
The reward, which is being administered through the State Department's Rewards for Justice national security program, also comes with "possible relocation" for the tipster.

The State Department said it is calling for "information about Iran's nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above."
Since the U.S. launched its war with Iran in February, President Trump has repeatedly reiterated that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon.

In its reward form, the State Department noted that according to the United Nations' International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran's uranium stockpile is believed to include uranium that has been enriched to 60% purity – "a level that is a short technical step from" the 90% level required to produce nuclear weapons.

"Iran is the only non-nuclear-weapon state to produce uranium at such a high enrichment level," the State Department said in its Rewards for Justice post. "Experts estimate this quantity, if enriched further, could be enough for several nuclear weapons."
Iran suspended IAEA inspections following on Iranian nuclear facilities by the U.S. and Israel.

"The regime's lack of compliance with the IAEA on safeguards obligations has led to the agency's loss of 'continuity of knowledge' regarding Iran's production and inventory of key components like centrifuges," the State Department said Friday.
U.S. coordinates with Canada to target Iranian digital asset providers
The Treasury Department on Friday targeted several firms exchanging Iranian rials and other currencies for allegedly helping Tehran evade sanctions and fund its proxies.
Some of the providers dealt with Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges already sanctioned by Washington.
The latest targets were coordinated with the Canadian government as several of the individuals and entities named are based in Vancouver and Toronto.
"Anyone, anywhere in the world, who helps Tehran evade sanctions risks being held accountable," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a statement.
Rubio to likely face questions about Iran at G7 foreign ministers meeting
Secretary of State Marco Rubio is set to embark on his first post-midterm foreign trip to attend a Group of Seven foreign ministers meeting in France next week.
He'll likely face questions about the Trump administration's policies, namely in Iran, after in elections that gave Democrats control of Congress.
The State Department said Friday that Rubio would travel to Paris to meet his counterparts from Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy and Japan on Monday and Tuesday.
Houthis say 30 people killed or wounded in Saudi strike on market
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis said Friday that a Saudi strike on a market in southwestern Yemen had killed or wounded 30 people.
The Houthis' Saba news agency said the "horrific massacre" had "resulted in the martyrdom and injury of more than 30 citizens."

The Houthis' political bureau said in a statement carried by Saba: "It is regrettable that these documented Saudi crimes have become like a forgotten file in the drawers of the United Nations and the so-called international community."
Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of killing and wounding "dozens of civilians" in attack on market

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels said Friday that the Saudi-led coalition fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognized government had targeted a market in the southwest of the country, killing and wounding "dozens of civilians."

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a post on X that Saudi aircraft struck the Al-Hadara market in the Taiz governorate on Friday "with three airstrikes, leaving dozens of civilians dead and wounded."
"These brutal crimes will not go unanswered and unpunished," he added.
The Saudi-led coalition said Friday, meanwhile, that air defense systems had intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis at Najran, a major city in southwest Saudi Arabia.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard say they have intercepted a U.S. drone in the Strait of Hormuz
Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed Friday to have destroyed another U.S. drone over Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
In a statement carried by the state TV network IRIB, the IRGC said a U.S. MQ-1 drone was "intercepted and destroyed over Qeshm Island by the IRGC's new advanced air defense system."

The IRGC claimed this was the 16th American MQ-1 drone it had intercepted during the war, and the second in two days. Iranian forces have also claimed to have shot down other U.S. drones, including more than two dozen of the more advanced, and more expensive MQ-9 Reapers.
Greek shipping firm says crew member killed in suspected missile strike on oil tanker
A seafarer was killed in an explosion caused by a suspected missile attack on an oil tanker Thursday in the Persian Gulf, a Greek company that manages the vessel said Friday.

The MT Velos Sapphire, a Marshall Islands-flagged tanker, which was not carrying cargo, was hit Thursday as it sailed toward Bahrain, management firm Velos Tankers said in a statement, according to Reuters.

"The company is greatly saddened to report the death of one of its seafarers, who was found fatally injured on board after having initially been reported missing in the aftermath of the explosion," the statement said.
Velos said, according to Reuters, that no crew members were injured and they managed to extinguish a fire on the ship caused by the blast.
The vessel was brought to Khalifa Bin Salman Port in Bahrain, and the damage to its hull was still being assessed, Reuters said.
Saudi-led coalition fighting Houthis in Yemen says drone intercepted in Mecca region

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis said Friday that it had intercepted a drone in the region of Mecca, Islam's holiest city, following repeated attacks on Saudi Arabia by the Yemeni rebels.
"Interception and destruction of a drone in the Mecca region," Turki al-Malki, the coalition's spokesman, wrote on X, without elaborating.

Since the breakdown of a truce in July, Saudi Arabia has traded blows with the Houthis, who have retaliated with strikes on Saudi airports, energy infrastructure and military sites that killed at least 20 people in October.
The Houthis have repeatedly denied targeting the holy cities of Mecca or Medina in Saudi Arabia and said they would not do so.
On Thursday, the Saudi coalition said it intercepted a missile fired by the Houthis at the Medina region, a claim rejected by the Iranian proxy group as a "blatant and grave falsehood."
CBS/AFP
Adviser to Iran's supreme leader says Tehran now "one of the main architects" of Mideast security
The Iranian supreme leader's adviser on international affairs, Aliakbar Velayati, said Friday that Iran was now "one of the main architects" of security in the Middle East.

Referring to how the U.S.-Iran war has changed the region in a series of posts on X, Velayati said that a "tsunami of geopolitical changes in West Asia swept up the Israeli and U.S. elections," and that "Iran is now one of the main architects of the regional order, a reality that cannot be erased or replaced."

Iran is a "bridge between the Persian Gulf, Central Asia, the Caucasus, and the Sea of Oman," he added, saying that "any energy or transit corridor seeking to bypass us will either be costly or unstable."

"The domino effect of crises, from Gaza to the Red Sea and from Lebanon to Iraq, has shown that regional security is indivisible," Velayati said. "Either collective security is achieved, or everyone will experience collective insecurity."
Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has not been seen in public since on Feb. 28.
Tanker hit by explosion in Strait of Hormuz, U.K. naval agency says
A tanker was hit by an explosion Thursday in the Strait of Hormuz, a British navy agency said Friday.

The master of a tanker leaving the Strait of Hormuz near Oman's coast reported "an explosion at the waterline" of the vessel, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center said, adding that the crew were all safe and the ship was "still under its own power and is continuing on its voyage."

Iran's state media reported Thursday that five oil tankers and a tugboat had caught on fire in or near the strait after hitting sea mines. It was unclear if the UKMTO report was in relation to one of those incidents claimed by Iran.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed Friday, in a statement carried by state media, that two more oil tankers had hit mines and caught on fire in or near the strait.
President Trump has accused Iran of lying about such incidents in an effort to drive up energy prices.
Trump holds a phone call with Qatar's emir, a key mediator in negotiations with Iran

President Trump called Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani to discuss efforts to end the U.S.-Iran war, a U.S. official confirmed to CBS News Friday, amid a diplomatic push to avoid a new round of major hostilities.

Their discussion, which the White House had not provided any information about by Friday morning, came as Iran's top diplomat made his own calls Thursday to counterparts across the Persian Gulf aimed at maintaining "stability in the region" amid concerns in many Gulf capitals that Mr. Trump will order major new U.S. strikes.

Al Thani received a call from Mr. Trump, according to a statement from the emir's office, during which the pair discussed "the latest regional developments, particularly diplomatic efforts aimed at de-escalating tensions in the region."
The emir "emphasized the importance of continuing dialogue and relying on diplomatic means to settle disputes and prevent further escalation," the statement said.
U.S. gas prices could soon dip below $4 a gallon. Why are fuel costs falling?
Motorists could soon see U.S. gas prices drop below $4 a gallon for the first time since July, according to energy experts.

Patrick De Haan, a petroleum analyst at price-tracking firm GasBuddy, told CBS News he expected the national average for gas, which the price-tracking firm put at $4.06 a gallon on Thursday and early Friday morning, to dip below the $4 threshold by next week. He also predicted diesel could fall below $6 a gallon by Thanksgiving.

Gas and diesel prices have both dropped over the last week, thanks largely to market expectations that the U.S. would underscore public dissatisfaction with the Iran war and pile pressure on the Trump administration to make a deal to end the conflict, De Haan said.
"Oil prices have been falling in the run-up to the election," he said. "My read is because there was optimism that after the midterms these problems would be addressed."
Saudi-led coalition intercepts 2 missiles launched by Houthis

The Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government said Friday that air defense systems had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels at Najran, a major city in southwest Saudi Arabia.
"Debris fell as a result of the interception, and damage assessment is underway," the statement said.
Iran says 2 tankers hit mines, caught fire in and near Strait of Hormuz

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement carried by state media Friday that two oil tankers hit mines and caught fire in or near the Strait of Hormuz, a day after Tehran claimed five other tankers had met similar fates.

"Two violating oil tankers — one east of the Strait of Hormuz and the other within the Strait itself — that attempted to transit via an unauthorized route struck mines," the IRGC said in a statement, according to state news outlets.

"These two tankers had deactivated all their navigation and identification systems. Supported by the aggressive and terrorist U.S. military, they attempted to exit the Strait of Hormuz via an unauthorized path; however, upon striking mines, they caught fire and were immobilized," the statement said.
On Thursday, Iranian media reported that five oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz in similar incidents.
There has been no confirmation of any of the incidents from maritime officials, and President Trump has accused Iran of making up such attacks to drive up global energy prices.

A U.K. naval agency said earlier this week, however, that despite repeated assurances from the U.S. that shipping lanes through the strait are open and safe, there were at least 30 attacks on commercial vessels in the region during October alone, a record high.

Since the war began with joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, Tehran has sought to control traffic through the strait, a key passage through which, before the war, about a fifth of global crude oil supplies would typically pass. In response, the U.S. imposed a blockade on Iranian ports.

The U.S. military has escorted tankers through the strait, which, along with other routes has helped bring shipments from the Gulf back up to or at least near to pre-war levels, but ships continue coming under attack.
CBS/AFP
Putin and Iran's security chief discuss building an oil pipeline from Russia to Iran

Russian President Vladimir Putin met Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei in Moscow Thursday to discuss strengthening ties between the two countries, including with the potential construction of a pipeline for Iran to import Russian gas.
Speaking with journalists after their meeting, Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, called it "an extremely important exchange," according to the Iranian embassy in Moscow.
"During the meeting with Mr. Vladimir Putin, discussions were held regarding the construction of gas pipelines from Russia to Iran," Rezaei was quoted as saying by Iranian state TV.
He noted the aim was to enable Iran "to address its own gas shortages while also facilitating the sale of Russian gas to neighboring countries."
Despite being a major producer, Iran has long suffered natural gas shortages, which have been exacerbated by the war with the United States and Israel.
During the most intense phase of the fighting, which lasted nearly 40 days, the U.S. and Israel struck key Iranian infrastructure including natural gas refineries, according to Tehran.
CBS/AFP
Trump touts imminent decision on whether he'll order new strikes on Iran
President Trump said Thursday that people will soon know his decision on whether to order a new round of U.S. strikes on Iran.
Mr. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that he believed it would take Iran 25 years to rebuild the country from the damage already inflicted during the war.
The president said he didn't want to bring further destruction to the country, but he may not have a choice.

Mr. Trump kept the possibility of a major new U.S. assault on Iran on the table in the run-up to the midterm elections this week, but hadn't renewed the threat since his Republican Party's dismal performance in the vote, which he acknowledged was, at least in part, a repudiation of the war.
Mr. Trump told the Financial Times newspaper on Tuesday evening, as U.S. ballots were counted, that he had no immediate plans to order new strikes on Iran.

articles.headline: ‘Fear and vitriol’: Democrats trash Stephen Miller as new Trump chief of staff
keyFacts: Incoming Democratic lawmakers and one Republican congressman are criticizing President Donald Trump for appointing Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff.
Critics argue Miller's promotion contradicts Trump's stated willingness to work with incoming Democrats and doubles down on controversial immigration policies.
Sen. Bernie Sanders stated he is not worried about the promotion, suggesting Trump might still be open to working with Congress on issues like raising the minimum wage.
body: Incoming Democratic lawmakers are slamming President Donald Trump’s choice to tap Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles as his highest-ranking staff member.

Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul el Sayed of Michigan decried Miller’s promotion as part of “incoherent messaging” from the Trump administration, arguing the choice runs contrary to Trump’s statements that he’s willing to work with incoming Democrats elected in 2026 midterms.

“Why appoint this man White House chief of staff if you want to have a productive relationship with the Congress that actually intends to deliver on the mandate that the American public has just given us? And we’ll wait to see,” el Sayed said on ABC’s This Week .

Democrats have slammed Miller, Trump’s longtime immigration adviser, for his influence over Immigration and Customs Enforcement policy, while the president’s Make America Great Again base has bolstered Miller and touted his policies cracking down on illegal immigration.

El Sayed questioned Miller, saying on Sunday, “I don’t know what Stephen Miller has actually contributed to our culture, our society, in any real way, except for to make us more angry, to stoke the worst kind of fear and vitriol, to weaponize ICE in our streets, to take American lives.”

Democratic Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton of Kansas also criticized Miller’s appointment to chief of staff, saying it is a “doubling down” on the policies of the first two years of the Trump administration.

“I’m actually surprised that he did that because the election was a repudiation of so much of what Trump has stood for, and I think so much of that was designed by Stephen Miller. So the idea of making him chief of staff seems really odd to me, and it’s concerning,” Hamilton said on CNN’s State of the Union .

One Republican congressman also ridiculed Trump’s decision to boost Miller on Sunday. Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-IN), who won his reelection campaign on Tuesday, said on CNN’s Inside Politics that Miller is “not liked out here in the Midwest.”
“If your team takes a beating as badly as we took this last week, you have to fire people. You don’t promote those who are, who were in charge of what was supposed to be delivered,” Stutzman said.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT), however, said he is “not worried” about Miller’s promotion. He told NBC’s Meet the Press that Trump is “mentally unbalanced, erratic, but he’s not stupid, and he is a good politician.”
TRUMP SIGNALS NO RETREAT FROM MAGA AGENDA WITH STEPHEN MILLER PROMOTION
“I think, when Trump looks out in the world and he sees millions of people working for starvation wages, he might not be unsympathetic to raising the minimum wage to a living wage,” Sanders said .
“I’m not worried about Miller. Do I think we can work with Trump? Maybe. I’m by no means guaranteeing it. But it is certainly worth the effort,” Sanders said.
