articles.headline: Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt
keyFacts: At least seven people died and more than 100 were injured after two trains collided near Giza in Egypt, causing carriages to derail.
Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi ordered an investigation to hold negligent parties accountable, while local hospitals went on heightened alert.
Trains between Giza and Upper Egypt were suspended while authorities worked to remove the wreckage.
body: - Published
At least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.
The country's railway authority said two trains travelling south from Giza and Cairo collided, causing several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment.
Images from the scene showed people looking inside overturned carriages for injured passengers as a massive emergency response was launched.
Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered state authorities to "investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".
The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.
The government said hospitals in the area had been put "on heightened alert" as they dealt with a massive influx of patients.
Egypt's health minister Dr Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said people were being treated for broken bones and head injuries.
The Egyptian Red Crescent said it was providing aid and psychological support to victims and their families at the scene.
The driver of one of the trains was among those who died in the crash, the ministry confirmed.

The first train involved in the crash was travelling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, when it crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to Aswan, which was stationary on the tracks.
Images from the scene showed some carriages had overturned, with the body of at least one appearing to have split in two.
Trains between Giza and the Upper Egypt region were suspended as cranes were dispatched to remove the wrecked trains. The railway authority has not said how long it expects this to take.

The collision occurred in the area between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat, close to where Egypt's deadliest train tragedy occurred in February 2002, when a fire engulfed a passenger train travelling from Cairo to Luxor.
In that incident, more than 370 people were officially reported killed, although some estimates put the toll considerably higher.
Two further crashes in the area in 2009 killed dozens more.
There were calls in Egypt on Sunday for the transport minister to resign over the latest deadly rail disaster.
Foreign leaders and dignitaries have shared condolences and support for the victims.
Saudi Arabia's ministry of foreign affairs expressed "solidarity" with Egypt and wished those hurt a speedy recovery.
Turkey's ambassador to Egypt wrote on X that he extended "heartfelt condolences and sincere sympathy" to the victims, their families, and the Egyptian people.

articles.headline: After GOP's brutal midterms, ‘Chuck Norris of Florida politics’ tells party to 'get up and fight'
keyFacts: Florida Lieutenant Governor Jay Collins urged Republicans to recover and fight after what Governor Ron DeSantis called devastating midterm election losses.
Collins said Florida serves as a blueprint for national Republicans, stating the party must better communicate with unaffiliated voters.
Collins is termed out of office in January and said he will evaluate his future in the state or national party.
body: When an insurgent's bullet shattered his arm in combat, Republican Florida Lt. Gov. Jay Collins did not wait around for an evacuation team; the Green Beret performed emergency surgery on himself to save the limb.

After the midterms that Gov. Ron DeSantis called a "near extinction-level" event for Republicans, Collins sees a national GOP lying bloodied on the field. He advises his battered and beaten party to show the same refusal to die, and get up like a warrior.

"Where we go from here is up to us as a Republican Party," Collins, dubbed the "Chuck Norris of Florida politics" by DeSantis, told Fox News Digital in an interview just days after the midterm "bloodbath."

"This can be a definitive death blow if we allow it to be, but I believe in what we stand for." he continued. "I believe in our Constitution. I believe in our founding fathers' vision. I believe that God blessed this nation. I think we have to knuckle down, learn, apply this, and we have come out with a relentless dedication and fury to focus on what matters: To lead our state, to lead our country, and be what we need to be for the American people. That is what we should choose to do."
"Hard times happen. Warriors, leaders get up and fight. That's what we have to do now."
DESANTIS CALLS GOP MIDTERM LOSSES 'EXTINCTION-LEVEL EVENT' — AND EXPLAINS WHY FLORIDA SURVIVED
The metaphor is not subtle. It is a road map, set forth by DeSantis' two four-year terms – the last year of which was supplemented by Collins as his No. 2.
HUGH HEWITT: THE GOP IS WOUNDED, NOT DEAD — BUT RECOVERY HAS TO START NOW
Collins said his home state's recent history of going from a purple state to a GOP stronghold is an example the rest of the country can follow.

"Florida's been the road map," he said. "I think we've been what I call the conservative proving grounds. I think that it's time for many here in Florida to use our voice and to be out there and help our party get back on their feet. Be resilient. Yeah, man, you got popped. You got hurt. Get back up, dust it off, and let's go lead. Let's learn."

While congressional Republicans scramble to assign blame for a devastating cycle of national losses – including the loss of Texas to Democrats – Florida has positioned itself as the country’s preeminent conservative fortress, now the largest red state on the 2028 map.

"Losing sucks, winning is awesome: Let's get back to more winning," he said. "We've just got to figure out how we're going to do that, and that's achievable. I think Florida is a blueprint. I think we have a responsibility to lead."
DAVID MARCUS: HOW ASHLEY MOODY SURVIVED THE BLUE TSUNAMI AND EMERGED AS A GOP STAR

Under DeSantis, Florida shed its long-held "purple" swing-state identity to become the nation's largest, most disciplined red bastion. Collins looked back on how he pulled in the no party affiliated voters (NPAs), the valued middle that can flip races and states, in his state Senate race before being tapped to serve under DeSantis.

"Republicans showed up, but the NPAs showed up and they overwhelmingly did not align with Republicans," Collins said, admitting that even Florida's heavy Republican registered voter edge led to slim margins in the tough midterm environment. "What does that tell us? Well, the biggest gap we had was that we didn't spend enough time communicating to our NPAs."
Collins pointed back to how he won a Tampa race in a district "that is not a conservative juggernaut in terms of Florida," running against the Tampa mayor's mother-in-law.

"This was my very first race," he recalled. "We didn't talk to a single Republican out there. We only knocked NPA's and light D's, and we won by 10. What does that tell you? In a community like Tampa, I didn't hide from my views. I told people I'm conservative, I'm a Republican."
JASON CHAFFETZ: FIVE TIMELESS POLITICAL LESSONS THAT GOT LOST IN 2026

"What I realized is if you're honest with people, you agree on more than you don't, but you have got to be willing to step in there and have that conversation," he said. "And we did that over and over and again. And we built a base of people who trust us, because I don't play games."
"As a party, we need to go back to being the party that welcomes folks in – a little bit more of a big tent – but we have to stand on our conservative values," he added.

Collins is termed out of office along with DeSantis in January, but he will evaluate his future in the state or the national party apparatus. For now, he is committing to nothing and merely saying, "Stay tuned."
TREY GOWDY: THE MIDTERMS WERE A PAINFUL LESSON THAT REPUBLICANS CAN'T SKIP LEARNING
Regardless of candidate or party, Collins goes back to his military background and having risked his life and literally sacrificed limb for unity.

"I wore a flag on my shoulder every single day that I served in uniform," he said. "I wore the flag on my suit, really every single day that I was out there, serving in our state or serving our nation in any way that I could. We're the American people; we are blessed."
Once the party picks its 2028 candidate , Republicans need to be all-in against the opposition, Collins said.

"We have to row the boat," he said. "Sept. 11 was a big day in our life. Sept. 12 was incredible because we saw the power and the might of what America can be. When we rowed the boat, our enemy was fearful. They were on their heels because they saw an absolute juggernaut standing righteously to defend our people and our way of life. What our enemy fears, what other nations fear is Americans coming together."
TRUMP-BACKED BYRON DONALDS TO MAKE HISTORY AS FLORIDA’S FIRST BLACK GOVERNOR

"We have to come together and realize that our nation is blessed," he continued. "It will fall if we don't come together. But it won't happen if we don't start uniting and remind ourselves that this is America, we're allies, internal in our country, and we're going to make sure that it's the greatest country moving forward. America's worth fighting for."

"We need to focus on getting through this, the aftermath of this cycle, wrap it up, transition, and make sure that we understand exactly what happened," he concluded. "You know, when we started the war on terror, and I was a young soldier, we spent two years trying to fight the last war. It wasn't very great, to be honest with you.

"Let's not fight the last war. Let's understand the operational environment. Let's under our gaps. Our weaknesses and how we can clearly address those. And then we're going to have to move with a righteous fury."

The draw against Villa extends Man Utd's winless run in the league to eight games - a club record in the Premier League era - raising further doubts over Carrick's position heading into the two-week November international break.
When questioned on his future by Sky Sports' Patrick Davison, Carrick engaged in a tetchy back-and-forth, insisting he would remain in charge.
PD: "What do you expect to happen over the next few weeks? If you thought walking away was the best thing, you'd probably do it."
MC: "It's not going to happen, no."

MC: "Is there?"

MC: "Would you?"

PD: "I'm asking you what you think? What do you expect to happen?"

MC: "We understand the situation; we haven't won enough games. But I expect to move forward and keep working on things we've been working on, showing a lot of the good in the game today, tighten up on a few mistakes and win football matches."
Then, speaking in his post-match press conference, Carrick expressed confidence his side could still turn things around this season.

"One hundred per cent," he said. "I think there's more than enough. Goals change games and we've got to deal with it and it's something we have to improve on drastically. But there's more than enough, we're just making it too difficult for ourselves at the moment in certain times…
"I'm quite clear with what direction the club needs to go in. We've just got to win games."
"Football is about moments, football is about what happens in both boxes in the end," Carrick added.

"Take (away) the moments and the totally avoidable goals we've given away, I actually thought we played pretty well, we were the better team for the most part and I'm disappointed we haven't won the game."
Neville: 'Ownership don't have a clue what to do' on Carrick
Sky Sports' Gary Neville on NBC:
"You can keep changing the manager and thinking that's going to be the answer. But this has been proven now over eight managers in 12 years - that's not the answer.
"Michael could leave, Michael might stay, we don't know. The ownership don't have a clue what to do.

"It's rinse and repeat. (Ruben) Amorim, (Erik) Ten Hag, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Carrick, Jose Mourinho, Louis van Gaal, David Moyes, Ralf Rangnick - some of them are world-class managers who have had success; there are a lot of promising young managers there, ex-players who know the club as well.

"None of it has worked because if you recruit badly, if you've got a poor performance department, a poor recruitment department, you've not got leadership that is strong right through the spine of the football club, you will fail.

"Every organisation in the world will fail if you've not got an aligned leadership from top to bottom - your board and your ownership right the way through to the person who is stood on the pitch trying to play football.
"There are real issues within that football club; you've got people doing those jobs who have never done those jobs before in senior positions."
Keane: 'Politician' Carrick 'better get moving' on improvements
Sky Sports' Roy Keane:
"It's obviously difficult for the manager. Under pressure, no doubt. He talks a lot but doesn't say much. I don't know if that's a tactic. Like a politician.
"He keeps saying we need to tighten up and there's things we need to work on, but they better get moving on that.
"It's the worst start in how many years; all these stats aren't very good. If you keep giving up goals and chances, it's just going to continue.
"What are we expecting to change over the next few weeks and months? What are they working on? They need to do a lot better than that."

articles.headline: California’s new insurance czar reveals massive overhaul to entire industry in the state: ‘No more’
keyFacts: Jane Kim declared victory in California's insurance commissioner race after proposing a public, nonprofit wildfire insurance fund.
Seven major property insurers have limited or paused new California policies as premiums surged 84% since 2020.
Kim said she expects first-year progress, but establishing the program will require working with state lawmakers and community leaders.
body: Jane Kim, a former San Francisco supervisor who defeated fellow Democrat Ben Allen in the race for insurance commissioner, declared victory Friday after campaigning on a plan to wrestle control of wildfire coverage away from private insurers and create a state-run, nonprofit alternative.
“We are here to say no more. We are going to make insurance work for us again,” Kim told supporters at her victory event.

Thanks for signing up!
“We are going to take on this $3-trillion industry because they have been profiting for way too long by raising our premiums, canceling our coverage and fighting our claims.”
Kim’s proposal, dubbed “Natural Disaster Insurance for All,” would separate wildfire coverage from traditional homeowners insurance policies and move it into a public, nonprofit fund.

The program would make wildfire insurance available to every current California homeowner, with premiums going toward providing coverage rather than executive compensation, shareholders or corporate advertising.
“The idea is that every current homeowner would be covered, and it would be a nonprofit fund where premiums don’t have to go to CEO pay, shareholders and Super Bowl ads,” Kim said.

The ambitious proposal comes as California grapples with an increasingly severe homeowners insurance crisis, with major carriers retreating from the state and residents struggling to find affordable coverage.

Seven of California’s largest property insurers have limited or paused new homeowners policies in the state, shrinking the private insurance marketplace as wildfire risks and rising costs continue to threaten coverage.

Homeowners insurance premiums have surged 84% since 2020, according to Stanford research, while enrollment in the state’s FAIR Plan — the insurer of last resort for homeowners unable to secure coverage through traditional companies — has nearly tripled.

The plan now covers roughly 5% of California homes, up from less than 2%, highlighting how the insurance crunch has spread beyond traditionally fire-prone communities and into the broader housing market.
Kim’s proposed public fund would effectively create a separate safety net for wildfire coverage, rather than forcing homeowners to rely entirely on private insurers.

But turning the proposal into reality could prove difficult, requiring cooperation from state lawmakers and community leaders to establish the program and determine how it would be funded and administered.
“This office is not a dictatorship. We’re going to have to work with community leaders across the state to make our big ideas possible,” Kim said.
Despite the hurdles, the incoming commissioner-elect said she expects to make progress on affordability and availability during her first year in office.
“I really believe we’re going to have some wins in our first year because there is a lot of work that can be done to make insurance more affordable, more available and more fair,” she said.
Kim, 49, secured approximately 53% of the vote to Allen’s 47%, according to the Associated Press. Her victory margin has grown to approximately 400,000 votes as additional ballots were tallied.
Allen called Kim to congratulate her on the victory Friday morning before she announced the results to supporters at San Francisco’s Dolores Park.

The win hands Kim responsibility for overseeing one of California’s most troubled industries at a time when homeowners are facing mounting premiums, canceled policies and fewer options for protecting their properties.

Her proposed nonprofit disaster insurance system would represent a major departure from the state’s traditional insurance model — and one of the most consequential tests of her incoming administration.

articles.headline: Europe to join U.S.-brokered Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, defying Kremlin objections
keyFacts: European officials will attend U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, France's foreign minister said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov previously objected to European participation, insisting the trilateral meeting format had already been agreed.
Scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday, the talks will address postwar security, de-escalation, and humanitarian issues, envoy Steve Witkoff stated.
body: Europe to join U.S.-brokered Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, defying Kremlin objections

European officials will turn up for the U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in the United Arab Emirates this week, France's foreign minister said Sunday, days after the Kremlin had insisted there could be no role for European powers at the meeting.

"France will be there and will ensure that Europe's voice is heard," Jean-Noël Barrot told French radio. He did not say who would represent Paris, or whether French or other European officials would take part directly in negotiations, or simply observe.
The meetings, which are set to take place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, had previously been presented as a three-way session between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv.
The Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov had earlier ruled out a European role, saying the trilateral format had already been agreed.

Talking to a Russian news channel on Friday, he accused European governments of failing to decide who speaks for them, while acknowledging that security talks would at some point require Europe's involvement.
On Thursday, President Trump met Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev and said a coming agreement was "going to involve more than Ukraine," adding he could even say it "might involve all of Europe."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told CNN on Friday that he had not been given details of the agreement Trump had referenced, and warned: "For me, it's not simple, and it can be dangerous." He invoked the 1945 Yalta conference, where Allied leaders settled Europe's division without the involvement of several affected countries.
A stalled process restarts

This will be the fourth round of talks between the two warring nations brokered by the Trump administration, and the first since those in Geneva this February. Earlier U.S.-brokered meetings have made little progress, and the chances of a breakthrough have been reduced as the Trump administration focused on its war with Iran.

Moscow confirmed it would return to the negotiating table only following a visit by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg in October. Those talks saw Putin announce the release of an American prisoner from a Russian jail — an apparent Kremlin gesture to President Trump's earlier lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Ukraine was vehemently opposed to the fuel sales — arguing they helped replenish Moscow's war chest.

Witkoff has said the agenda for these latest talks will include postwar security arrangements and de-escalation of the conflict and humanitarian issues, shortly after Melania Trump helped broker a limited ceasefire that allowed humanitarian aid to enter a town inside Russian-occupied Ukraine.

Russia's delegation will again be led by Vladimir Medinsky, a hardline Putin aide who has participated in most talks with Ukraine since the unsuccessful first set of discussions all the way back in March 2022.

For the first time, these talks will also include Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, as well as Yury Zhigarlovsky, a deputy head of the General Staff's operations directorate, alongside military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov.

This more senior lineup could indicate that Moscow is readier than before to address thorny political and military questions. But the U.S. think tankInstitute for the Study of War suggested some of those same Russian officials have in fact previously sought to slow down previous talks or push harder on Moscow's demands.

The gaps between the two countries remain substantial. Russia has demanded that Ukraine give up large parts of its territory and renounce NATO membership. Zelenskyy has repeatedly insisted any security commitments should be clearly spelled out, including who would act, and how, if Russia attacked again.
Skepticism and shifting politics

Some analysts expect little. In an op-ed for the Atlantic Council think tank, the former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine John Herbst argued that Putin had rejected every U.S. proposal Kyiv accepted and preferred participating in peace talks than pursuing actual peace. "Perhaps the only outcome of the talks," he wrote, "will be to agree to another round."
The meetings in the United Arab Emirates also follow Democrats' midterm victories, which Zelenskyy said could improve Ukraine's chances of more U.S. aid.
Russia, too, may be looking to push for the Trump administration's outlines of a Ukraine deal — before a Democratic-controlled Congress arrives come January.

Also hovering over the talks — the prospect of Trump, Xi, and Putin gathering for a trilateral meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China later this month. While details remain murky, all sides have confirmed discussions are underway.
And as officials travel to Abu Dhabi to talk peace, the war has raged on regardless.
Zelenskyy said Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles at the Kyiv area overnight Saturday, with only four intercepted, accusing Moscow of treating diplomacy "as a form of aggression."
In southern Ukraine, the death toll from a guided-bomb strike Monday on an aid distribution site in Komyshuvakha rose to at least 55.

articles.headline: Hakeem Jeffries supports impeachment of Pete Hegseth: ‘He has got to go’
keyFacts: House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries announced he strongly supports an impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Republican Representative Thomas Massie prepared eight impeachment articles accusing Hegseth of offenses including violating the War Powers Resolution.
Massie plans to reintroduce the impeachment resolution on Monday, and House Democrats will discuss supporting it on Tuesday.
body: House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, poised to become majority leader, said on Sunday that he strongly supports impeaching defense secretary Pete Hegseth as a Republican lawmaker prepares to force a House vote.
The top Democrat made his position clear during an appearance on ABC’s This Week, declaring himself a “hard yes” on the impeachment resolution targeting Hegseth.

“I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution. The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe,” Jeffries said. “Pete Hegseth has got to go.”
The announcement comes as Kentucky Republican representative Thomas Massie, an outgoing congressman and frequent critic of Donald Trump, moves to revive his impeachment effort against Hegseth.

Massie said he plans to reintroduce an impeachment resolution as soon as Monday, potentially setting up a House showdown within days. The measure includes eight articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of multiple offenses, including violating the War Powers Resolution of 1973.

Asked whether he expects the entire Democratic caucus to support the resolution, Jeffries said members will “have that conversation” Tuesday morning when lawmakers return to Washington for the first time since the midterm elections.
“But I believe there will be incredibly strong support for that resolution,” Jeffries said.
The mounting pressure on Hegseth follows Republican losses in the midterm elections, with both Trump and voters identifying the Iran war as a major factor in the party’s defeat.

A former senior Pentagon official pointed directly to the defense department’s role in the conflict, saying Wednesday that the war “has been primarily a Department of War-led effort because you chose to take military action to resolve a foreign policy matter”.

“If the president is serious about anyone taking responsibility for it, it’s Pete Hegseth,” one Republican close to the White House added in an interview with CNN. “Pete has been either dishonest or incorrect – neither of which are acceptable – about timelines, goals and objectives since the beginning.”
Despite the criticism, Trump has continued to stand behind Hegseth. When reporters asked on Wednesday whether he was considering replacing Hegseth, the president dismissed the possibility.
“No, I think he’s doing a very good job,” Trump said.

Hegseth, meanwhile, pushed back against the impeachment effort in a video posted to social media on Thursday, accusing his political opponents of pursuing a politically motivated campaign against him.

“A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice,” Hegseth said. “It’s all about the politics of personal destruction – didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me.”

The impeachment push comes as Democrats prepare to intensify scrutiny of Hegseth’s tenure as defense secretary. Democrats have promised to investigate Hegseth and his handling of the Pentagon, and aides say that could include everything from his handling of the Iran war to his purges of top military officers, including the chair of the joint chiefs of staff.
He could also face scrutiny over his Ukraine policy and US military strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats in Latin American waters, which some Democrats say could amount to war crimes.

articles.headline: All vault locations in the Fortnite Chapter 7 mini season
keyFacts: Polygon reported that Fortnite Chapter 7's mini season features nine locked vaults containing rare chests and a sprite chest.
Polygon stated that players need a rare vault key found in chest loot to unlock these locations across the map.

body: Vaults are locked locations around the map that contain rare chests and a sprite chest in Fortnite Chapter 7's mini season.

To get into a vault, you need to find a vault key, which can be found randomly as chest loot. They're a bit rare, but they're worth holding onto if you're near a vault. However, vaults are a highly sought after commodity, and there are only so many of them.
Here's the location of every vault in Fortnite Chapter 7's mini season, so you know where to go as soon as you get a vault key.
All vault locations in Fortnite Chapter 7 mini season

There are nine vaults in Fortnite Chapter 7's mini season. To open one, you need to have a vault key. With the vault key equipped, the closest unopened vault that is in the storm will appear as a lock on your map. However, vaults in the storm might still be unopened, so if you have a ton of healing items, they still might be worth going to. Inside each vault, you'll find four rare chests and one rare sprite chest.
In the image above, we've marked the locations of every vault, and in the list below, we've detailed where you can find them.
- Head to the south side of the island with Rubber Resort, and you'll find this vault near the middle of the beach.
- Go behind the waterfall at Loot Lagoon to find this vault.
- At Lil' Uzi's Stronghold, you'll find a tall building with a mural of Lil' Uzi Vert. Go to its west side, and head inside the small blue-roofed section to find this vault.
- Head west of Lantern Landing and drop off the cliff. You'll find this vault in the wall.
- Go west of Cursed Cavern, and you'll find a small tower. Go under the west stairs to find this vault.
- Go to the lowest floor of The $.$. Rocky, and you'll find this vault on the south side.
- Head to the northwest side of the island with Windmill Village. You'll find a red house with a blue roof. Drop off the cliff to the north, and you'll find this vault in the wall.
- Go into the canals below Loguetown, and you'll find this vault.
- Head to the southwest area of Busy Bay, and you'll find a shipwreck on the beach. Face east, and you'll see a vault.

articles.headline: Skyrim lead designer Bruce Nesmith loved that Baldur's Gate 3 closed off story paths based on your decisions, but defends Bethesda's approach: 'They were both fun, they're just fun in different ways'
keyFacts: Skyrim lead designer Bruce Nesmith said he enjoyed how Baldur's Gate 3 closed off story paths based on player decisions.
Nesmith contrasted this with Bethesda's philosophy of letting players experience all guilds and content within a single playthrough.
Nesmith concluded that Bethesda and Larian approaches are both fun in different ways.
body: Speaking on a new episode of The Examined Game, Skyrim lead designer Bruce Nesmith shared his big takeaway from Baldur's Gate 3, and contrasted the approaches Bethesda and Larian have taken in their respective RPGs.

"The surprises come with the little things, not the big things. I have a long history with D&D as well as Bethesda. For me, it was joyful to see the D&D expression of fantasy rules come to life. Larian Studios did a magnificent job of that. I also thought that they redefined things in a certain way. Bethesda games have always had the philosophy of, let the player play everything.

"You can play the entire Thieves' Guild, you can play the entire Fighters' Guild, you can play the entire Mages' Guild, etc. There is nothing that your character can't play. That's a very good philosophy. I support that philosophy. But I was pleasantly surprised to see how positive it felt to me to make consequential decisions that closed off gameplay in Baldur's Gate.

"That also felt good, because it was done well. I felt like the decisions I made had more meaning in certain ways, because there were actual consequences. If I wanted to see those other [outcomes], I'd have to bring up another character and try different paths.

"They were both fun, they're just fun in different ways, and that, to me, was part of the surprise. I would have expected to fall on one side or the other, as if they were things [where] you couldn't have both. The lesson learned is: You can have both. I can enjoy this game over here that does it this way, and enjoy this game over here that does it that way."

I think Nesmith is 100% correct, and it's really Bethesda's lane to offer relatively unhindered fantasy fulfillment in its games. You generally see players and modders be the ones to introduce roleplaying-oriented restrictions, while Bethesda maximizes freedom.

At the same time, I've always thought that what separates Bethesda games from more pure sim sandboxes like Mount & Blade is that the studio provides the player with just enough structure and narrative to push back on. I think there's room to experiment there, and examples in Bethesda's own back catalogue of where it can take things.

Morrowind springs to mind: The Fighters' and Thieves' Guilds are opposed to each other, and their quests are mutually exclusive after a point—you even directly sabotage the other guild in each questline. The Mages' Guild and House Telvanni are similarly opposed, and the Dunmer Houses pretty much all hate each other.

But you don't even have to go all the way back to 2002: Skyrim has three major examples in the Civil War questline, the Dawnguard expansion, and the alternate ending to the Dark Brotherhood story. Siding with the Penitus Oculatus in "Destroy the Dark Brotherhood" isn't as substantial as the faction quest you're throwing away, but it is a very cool addition that enhances Skyrim's sense of depth and stakes. I'd love to see more like it in TES6: Sentinel—wouldn't it be rad to have a full questline for both the secret police and the assassins' guild?

I caught on Nesmith's choice of words that he enjoyed Baldur's Gate 3's approach "because it was done well." I've certainly encountered content-blocking choices in games that felt cheap or forced. I'm a huge CD Projekt fan, but I'll always be a hater when it comes to The Witcher 2's mutually exclusive second acts. I think the same idea was executed much better in Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty.

keyFacts: Dataminers found references to the Master Quest mode in the files for the new Ocarina of Time remake.
Dataminer OatmealDome stated that the mode will be unlocked by owning DLC and features a mirrored world and modified dungeons.
Nintendo has not officially announced DLC or the release of Master Quest for the remake.
body: Ocarina of Time's notoriously tricky Master Quest mode could be making a comeback in the new remake.
Dataminer MrCheeze shared a list of strings from the remake's files on Bluesky, several of which tie the tag "MQ" to dungeons like Dodongo's Cavern.
In a follow-up, as spotted by TheGamer, they pointed to further entries, including "HasMQ", "IsMQModeExist", "NewGameMQ", and "ReleaseMQ".

Fellow dataminer OatmealDome added on Twitter/X that the mode will be unlocked by owning DLC, rather than arriving in an update, though "the data is incomplete". "I can confirm that the world is mirrored and dungeons are modified (e.g. cows in Jabu-Jabu's Belly)," they said.
— MrCheeze (@mrcheeze.github.io) November 6, 2026 at 2:23 PM

If you've not played it, Master Quest is a remixed version of Ocarina of Time with rearranged dungeons and tougher puzzles. It first appeared as a bonus disc on GameCube, then came back in 2011's Ocarina of Time 3D, which unlocked it after you finished the main game. That version also mirrored the whole world, which matches what OatmealDome has found, and had enemies deal double damage.
[Ocarina of Time] #ootspoilers
There is data in the game files for Master Quest. It will be unlocked by *owning DLC* - it is not just an update.
The data is incomplete, but I can confirm that the world is mirrored and dungeons are modified (e.g. cows in Jabu-Jabu's Belly).
— OatmealDome (@OatmealDome) November 7, 2026

As with any datamine, there's no guarantee it'll ever see the light of day. Nintendo hasn't announced any DLC for the remake, and it's not clear whether Master Quest would be free, like it was on 3DS, or paid.

articles.headline: Government 'looking seriously' at banning under-16s from Vinted and eBay
keyFacts: Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy stated that the government is seriously considering banning under-16s from retail platforms like Vinted and eBay to protect children.
The proposed expansion responds to concerns that messaging functions on these online marketplaces allow strangers to groom children.
Both eBay and Vinted responded that they look forward to working constructively with the government and maintaining open dialogue.
body: - Published
Vinted and eBay could be included in the list of platforms set to be banned for children aged under 16, the culture secretary has said.
Lisa Nandy said the government was "looking seriously" at including the retailing websites in the social media ban "to keep children safe".
The UK's social media ban for under-16s is set to come into force in March next year, with children barred from accessing platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.

In response, eBay said it was looking forward to "understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government". Vinted said it welcomed "open dialogue" with ministers and the regulator on the issue.

Asked on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether the government was looking to ban under-16s from Vinted and eBay, Nandy said: "We are looking seriously at doing so in order to keep children safe."
It came after the Sunday Times reported, external that the UK's social media ban was being expanded to include the popular second-hand online marketplaces.

The move was due to fears that messaging functions on the platforms allowed strangers to groom children, according to the newspaper. It suggested similar reselling platforms, Depop and Facebook Marketplace, would also be included in the list of banned sites.

Businesses and individuals sell a host of goods on eBay, which has been a major global player in the online reselling market for years. The platform states on its website that it currently requires all of its members to be over 18 years old because listings involve "entering into a contract".
Vinted is aimed at over 18s, but its terms and conditions do allow parents or guardians to create accounts for their children, which must be used under parental supervision.
The site, on which users mostly buy and sell unwanted clothes and other fashion items, has grown rapidly recently to reach 17 million UK users.

A Vinted spokesperson said direct messaging was "part of how the platform works" but that it had a "zero tolerance for harmful or explicit content" and had moderation teams and tools to spot and remove "activity that breaks our rules".
"When we identify inappropriate behaviour, we take action, up to a permanent ban or reporting to the relevant authorities," they said.
An eBay spokesperson said the company was "focused on providing a trusted and safe marketplace experience for our millions of customers".
"While the details of the proposed legislation are not yet clear, we look forward to understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government," they added.
The government announced it would ban under-16s accessing social media in June this year, with children prevented from accessing 10 of the biggest platforms.
YouTube will also be banned for under-16s, but YouTube Kids - a version of the video-sharing app designed to be safe for children - will not be included in the measures.
A complete list of affected platforms has not yet been released, but the government said it would cover those "whose purpose is to enable social interaction and which allow users to post material".
That means platforms that have livestreaming or features that enable the potential for strangers to contact children will also be restricted, which includes gaming sites.

It does not mean that Roblox, the biggest gaming site in the UK for those aged eight to 12, for example, will be banned for under-16s. However, certain features such as its chat function will be restricted.
But Matthew Sinclair, a senior director at the Computer and Communications Industry Association, which represents tech companies, argued that ministers should prevent the rules having "scope creep".

He said a restriction on messaging for under-16s "would not stop at social media and would reach into the services families depend on to stay in touch", and urged the government to "ensure any new restrictions are proportionate and effective."
The UK's ban comes after a similar one was introduced in Australia last year.
Many children there have found ways to get round it, but the UK has said it intends to take a tougher approach.
In recent weeks, attention has turned to how a social media ban would be enforced.
Last month, the communications regulator Ofcom set out its recommendations for the most effective ways to identify which of the UK's millions of social media users are aged over 16.
Rani Govender, head of online child safety at the NSPCC, said the "real question" going forward was how the government ensured age checks were effective.

"But effective age checks are only part of the solution," she added. "Tech companies must also be required to build child safety into every platform, device and AI tool, so children are protected from harmful and illegal content and only able to access age-appropriate services."

body: As is always the case, there is no shortage of great games to play. That can make picking your favorites--or voting for categories in something like The Game Awards--a challenge. With this year's awards just about a month away, we're reflecting on what games we've loved this year to offer up some quick suggestions on what you should consider playing before casting your votes.

Below, we've rounded up one-sentence recommendations from our staff. Our goal here was twofold: recognize the games we're individually considering for Game of the Year, whether or not they're well-known, and also spotlight some of the smaller games we loved that you might have missed or never even heard of.

articles.headline: Why animals are smarter than we think
keyFacts: When I was growing up, one of my favorite things to hear from an adult was that I was smart.
It made me feel special — like I was capable of doing things that other people weren’t.
In hindsight, that pride came with baggage: pressure to do well academically, and a sense of competition that wasn’t always necessary.
body: When I was growing up, one of my favorite things to hear from an adult was that I was smart. It made me feel special — like I was capable of doing things that other people weren’t.

In hindsight, that pride came with baggage: pressure to do well academically, and a sense of competition that wasn’t always necessary. Like many, I grew out of it. But many people in power still have a preoccupation with intelligence and conventional ways of measuring it.

Now, though, the way that we think about intelligence and markers of it, such as IQ, are shifting in important ways. David Robson, the author of The Intelligence Trap: Why Smart People Make Dumb Mistakes , says that traditional markers like IQ are not the only factors when considering how smart someone is. “There’s practical intelligence, which is much more about how good you are at planning projects and executing those projects,” he explains. He even says that people with high IQs tend to be more susceptible to things like confirmation bias.

Philosopher Jeff Sebo goes further, arguing that even focusing our discussion of intelligence on people is too narrow. He’s the author of the book The Moral Circle: Who Matters, What Matters, and Why , and he says that making humans the bar for intelligence is a mistake. “Intelligence in general is the ability to process information and solve problems and adapt to the environment,” he told Vox. Animals’ brains “might not look exactly like ours, but they can help animals solve problems and navigate their environments and adapt to their situations really effectively.”
So what does animal intelligence actually look like? And what can we learn from it? We answer that and more on this week’s episode of Explain It to Me , Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.

Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Sebo, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
What is it about one animal’s intelligence that makes us want to protect it versus another animal that can end up on our dinner table? I think of dogs versus cows and pigs or dolphins versus fish.

There are many factors that shape how much empathy we have for non-human animals of various kinds. Are they cute and do they look like us? Do they remind us of ourselves? What role do we assign them in our lives?

We have more empathy by default for animals who play companion roles in our lives as opposed to animals who play commodity roles in our lives. This is why we can often have much more empathy for some animals over others, even if they display the same markers of sentience and the same markers of intelligence.
What’s a discovery about an animal’s mind that might surprise people? That might make us think of that animal differently than we maybe do?

There are really interesting studies showing that bees are capable of play behaviors. You can go online and see a video of a bee rolling a wooden ball around in a way that displays all the hallmarks of play activity. This is done seemingly for the pure joy of rolling a wooden ball around.

Likewise, there are studies showing that animals like insects have remarkable capacities for perception and learning and memory and adaptive, flexible decision-making and communication with each other. Animals that we might have written off as simple, as mechanistic, are in fact incredibly complex, seemingly sensitive, seemingly intelligent. I think that has allowed people to have a little bit more empathy for some of these animals than they otherwise might.

How much of what we call animal intelligence is actually just animals doing the things that people happen to be good at? What kind of abilities are we overlooking when we think of animals and intelligence?

We do tend to look for markers of intelligence that we associate with human intelligence and that can sometimes lead us to overlook markers of specifically non-human intelligence. This can happen in so many different ways.

For example, for many years, the gold standard for self-awareness tests was a mirror self-recognition test. You would put a mark on the forehead of an animal and place them in front of a mirror and see if they notice the mark and if they try to remove the mark and that can signal a certain kind of self-awareness.

It took us a long time to appreciate that this might not be the best way to test self-awareness in many animals for a variety of reasons. Many animals are not primarily visual, so we might need to think about how to perform this kind of test with their sensory modalities. Also, many animals might not particularly care about whether they have a mark on their forehead, so we should probably not treat an attempt to remove that mark as a standard for self-awareness.

We hear that pigs are intelligent or that octopuses could solve puzzles and we think, “Oh wow, we should be treating these creatures better.” I wonder, is there a problem with that argument? Because what happens to the animals that just never impress us?

I think that learning more about animal intelligence and challenging our preconceived notions about animals is good, but I think it would be a mistake to treat a certain level of intelligence — and especially a certain level of human-like intelligence — as a necessary condition for moral consideration.

That might lead us to extend respect and kindness to elephants and chimpanzees and other relatively human-like animals while neglecting the other animals who are conscious and sentient, capable of feelings and emotions, and that have forms of agency and decision-making, even if it might not look like ours.
I think that bar should be lower and should at the very least include consciousness and sentience.
This is making me realize that I may not be clear on what it means to be sentient. How do we know if an animal’s sentient or not?

This is very difficult to know for sure, because sentience is the capacity for positive and negative experiences like pleasure, pain, happiness, and suffering. The only experiences that any of us can directly experience are our own.

With non-human animals, we can collect behavioral evidence, internal evidence, developmental evolutionary evidence. For example, behaviorally, we can ask, “Do they nurse their own wounds? Do they respond to analgesics and antidepressants the way that we do?” And then developmentally, evolutionarily, we can ask, “In their ancestral environments, did they face pressures that they could overcome if they developed the ability to experience pleasure, pain, happiness, and suffering?” None of this is proof, none of it establishes certainty, but when we find a lot of this evidence in an animal, that at least increases the probability.

In terms of ethics and policy, what matters is we should not wait for certainty that someone can suffer before taking basic steps to address welfare risks for them. If there is at least a realistic possibility that someone can suffer based on the evidence, then we should take reasonable proportionate steps to mitigate welfare risks for them when we make decisions that affect them.

I personally don’t think of plants as sentient, but one of the things I love about my monstera is whenever it’s moved around in my apartment, it turns itself towards the sun. Does it make sense to call them intelligent when they do things like that?

At least in a certain broad sense, I think that it does. Plants are remarkably sophisticated. Many plants have capacities for perception, for collecting information from the environment, for learning and memory, for retaining some information, for communication, sending signals to other nearby plants, and even for adaptive decision-making, for growing toward things that are good for them and away from things that are bad for them.

Now, this might not mean that plants are sentient, but whether or not it feels like anything to be a plant, they might still be agentic and intelligent in the sense of being able to process some information, being able to adapt to their environment in some ways. I think that can be worth acknowledging.
What would that change about our world and how it functions?
I think that if we seriously considered non-human sentience and welfare, then it would have transformative implications for how we live, but ones that could be very good for humanity as well.

Consider how we relate to food and consider how we relate to wildlife. On the food side, industrial animal agriculture is a leading driver of animal suffering, but then it is also a leading driver of public health and environmental risks for humans. It creates more antibiotic resistance, more disease outbreaks, more extreme weather events via climate change, more biodiversity loss via deforestation.

Similarly, we build an infrastructure primarily for humans, and that can lead to a lot of unnecessary conflict with wildlife. Wildlife can die because they fly into buildings or fly into cars or are trapped in light pollution or trapped in parks with no exit for them if there is a flood or a fire.

If we simply considered their interests when building our infrastructure, then we might be able to build an infrastructure that can be good for human and non-human residents at the same time. But it does require considering human and non-human interests together when making decisions that affect everybody.

articles.headline: Physicists listened to electrical noise to crack a superconductor mystery
keyFacts: Physicists led by Milan Allan and Ingmar Swart studied electrical noise in cuprates to investigate high-temperature superconductivity.
Researchers investigated the pseudogap phenomenon, where electrons seem to vanish above superconducting temperatures, with two competing explanations proposed.
Scientists sought a direct way to observe electron pairs to resolve decades of inconclusive experimental readings regarding the superconductor mystery.
body: Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, but most only work a few degrees above absolute zero. In the late 1980s, copper-based materials called cuprates were found to superconduct at higher temperatures—reachable with affordable liquid nitrogen. Yet nearly 40 years later, physicists still don’t agree on why.

In a recent Science study, a team of physicists led by Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University in the Netherlands has found some answers by listening to the faint electrical crackle of current flowing into a cuprate.
The missing electrons

Central to the mystery of cuprates’ high-temperature superconductivity is a strange state called the pseudogap. “The pseudogap is a phenomenon of missing electrons,” Allan said. Above the temperature at which cuprates become superconducting, some of their electrons seem to vanish—measurements find far fewer of them at the energies where they should be. “Everybody knows that from different probes, you see that there’s these vanishing electrons, but nobody knows why,” Allan said.

Over the decades, physicists have put forward two main competing explanations. The first hypothesizes that the electrons get stuck in some sort of structure. In this view, electrons freeze into patterns, such as charge density waves, and superconductivity develops separately. The alternative explanation tightly links this phenomenon to superconductivity. “Other people think they’re missing because they form pairs,” Allan said. Pairs of electrons, called Cooper pairs, are what carry current in a superconductor. If, as the material cools, these pairs appear before the material becomes superconducting, they would be a precondition of superconductivity, a waiting room of sorts, where pairs exist but can’t yet move together in lockstep.

Settling this proved extremely hard. “Lots of different experimental signatures are kind of lumped inside this,” Allan said. Different instruments all see something, but their readings, Allan said, are never conclusive. “It’s always something kind of incoherent, hard to grasp,” he said. What the researchers needed was a way to see pairs directly, and Allan and his colleagues figured it out.

articles.headline: Parents, sister of far-right Kraków shooter found dead in family home
keyFacts: Police said three bodies found in the family home of a 24-year-old gunman in Kraków belonged to his parents and sister.
The suspect, described as having far-right views, killed six people in a mass shooting in Kraków and remains hospitalized in critical condition.
Investigators are probing the suspect for murder regarding both the city center attack and the deaths of his relatives.
body: Three bodies found in the home of the 24-year-old shooter in the Saturday’s rampage in the heart of Kraków belonged to the gunman’s family, police said.

Investigators are looking at the deaths of the shooter’s parents and sister as they unravel events surrounding the random violence in the Polish city’s historic center, Main Market Square, around 3 p.m. on Saturday.
The relatives, who lived about 90 miles from Krakow, likely died from gunshot wounds, according to police.
Authorities said the shooter, who survived a shootout with police and remains in the hospital, wore a bulletproof vest during the attack.

The identifications were made as world leaders paid tribute to victims and Poland declared two national days of mourning after a shooter motivated by far-right ideologies killed six people in Kraków on Saturday, in what the country’s defense minister characterized as a “terror attack.”

Victims of the attack included a man from the United Kingdom, a woman from Austria and four Polish nationals, according to regional official Krzysztof Jan Klęczar. The injured included visitors from Britain, Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria, according to the Associated Press.
St. Mary’s Basilica in the square paused its hourly trumpet call overnight in honor of the victims. It was the first time the historic church had done so since World War II.

The gunman, described by officials as having “ultranationalistic” beliefs, is reported to have opened fire in Kraków’s main market square. Four women and two men were killed in the midday attack, the country’s deadliest shooting in decades, while a policeman who confronted the gunman is in critical condition.

The suspect is being investigated on suspicion of murder in connection with the six deaths, Polish Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said on X Sunday, adding that he “acted with the aim of seriously intimidating a large number of people, making this a terrorist offence.”

The same suspect is facing a separate murder charge over killings in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyskie, Żurek said, a town some 93 miles northeast of Kraków where three of the man’s relatives were found dead in his home.

“Establishing all the circumstances of these tragic events, determining the full sequence of the perpetrator’s actions and securing evidence are currently the priorities of the investigation,” which is being led by terror offense specialists within the prosecutor’s office, he said.
Krakow‘s prosecutor Eryk Stasielak said the shooter was in critical condition and victim autopsies were set to start on Monday, according to PAP, a Polish news service.
“Tomorrow we will be deciding the fate of the attacker, if he survives, because he remains in critical condition,” Stasielak said, according to a translation of the report.

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński did not name the suspect but identified him as a Polish national in his mid-20s from Ostrowiec Świętokrzyskie. He used an automatic rifle, Kierwiński said Saturday, describing him as having “ultranationalistic” views.
“Everything indicates he was fascinated by far-right ideologies,” he said.
The suspect was shot by police at the scene and taken to the hospital around 3 p.m. local time. He remains in critical condition, regional governor Krzysztof Klęczar told a news conference Sunday.
A man and two women later found dead in an apartment are believed to be the suspect’s parents and sister, according to Andrzej Fijołek, deputy inspector of Police National Headquarters.
Two national days of mourning on November 8 and 9 were announced by the Interior Ministry on Sunday.

Pope Leo XIV issued a message to the archbishop of Krakow on Sunday expressing sadness over the tragedy. The Pope “implores the gift of Christian hope for the families overwhelmed by grief and joins with all those experiencing these days of mourning,” the message read, according to a translation.
Żurek, the justice minister, said on social media early on Sunday that Senior Constable Jakub Kulik “is fighting for his life in hospital” after he confronted the shooter.
“One of his lungs is not functioning, and he needs every drop of blood he can get,” he posted on X.
Police later said that blood banks in Kraków were full and thanked those who donated.
“Senior constable Jakub Kulik and senior constable Artur Moranski are true heroes,” said Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said, referring to both policemen.
Klęczar said that without “the efficient and selfless intervention” of the officers, “the number of victims could have been significantly higher.”
“The condition of the two police officers remains serious,” Klęczar said Sunday, though Kierwiński later said the two men had been brought out of comas.

Video posted on social media shows what appears to be an injured police officer firing at the gunman before dropping to his knees and rolling over onto his back. The officer, who did not appear to have backup nearby, is seen struggling to reload his firearm and appeared to be clutching his right arm.

Four of the dead in the city center attack have been identified, though their names have not been released. They include four Polish nationals, a British national, and one non-Polish woman whose nationality has not yet been publicized, Klęczar said.
All those wounded were alive on Sunday, he said, adding that 11 of the 16 injured people are Polish and two of the individuals are police officers.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the U.K. government “deeply mourns the British national and other victims” who died in the shooting.
“The U.K. stands resolutely in solidarity with the people of Poland,” he said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also said Saturday that his country “stands in solidarity” with neighboring Poland, calling the shooting a “shocking crime.”
The U.S. State Department said it was not aware of any American citizens harmed in the violence.
“The profound depth of Poland’s shock at the horror of yesterday’s appalling mass murder in Krakow is truly remarkable to behold,” U.S. Ambassador to Poland Tom Rose said in a post on X.

Noting how rare the incident was in a “extraordinarily safe” country like Poland, he added: “There’s something profoundly precious about being in a country where such evil remains so foreign to everyday life, where an entire nation recoils in horror at the mere thought of it, and where the depth of grief reveals the true goodness of its people.”
Part of Main Market Square in Kraków and surrounding streets reopened Sunday, but cordons remain in place while police carry out forensic work, the city has said in a statement.
Several makeshift memorials with flowers and candles appeared across the city on Sunday.
Tourists caught up in attack
Many of those caught up in the attack were tourists visiting the city.

Taylor Dorfmeister, a 21-year-old American student studying in Italy who was visiting Poland, was in the square with his roommate when gunfire erupted. Dorfmeister said there was a delay before the crowd reacted and then everyone began to flee the area. He said he took shelter in a building.
“We ran up the stairs in the building to hide and it was a dead end, which is when I was the most terrified since the gunshots were [loud] and near,” Dorfmeister told NBC News.

It sounded to Dorfmeister like the gunfire was coming from the first floor of the building where he hid. The student from Santa Cruz, California, was “fully prepared for the worst” based on the proximity of the noise, he said.
“This is it,” Dorfmeister thought. “Like, there’s nowhere to go, nowhere to hide.”
Marie-Ange Collaer was visiting with her family from Brussels.

“We literally ran for our lives and managed to hide from the bullets flying around,” she wrote on Facebook. “Lying on the floor in a shop like in a bad police movie whilst you hear bullets everywhere.”
Collaer said her family was shaky and “quite in shock” after returning to their hotel but everyone was grateful to be alive.
“We saw a few that did not make it, true horror,” she wrote.
U.K. resident Neil Thaxton and his wife, Nicky, also survived the attack.

“We had just walked through the main square and heard the gunshots,” Thaxton wrote on Facebook. “We thought it was fireworks then people started running, we went into a gift shop and the staff took us in the back of the shop and locked the doors and turned the lights off.”

articles.headline: Doom delivers five minutes of terminal violence on an IBM mainframe
keyFacts: WND Software created a browser demo that allows users to play Doom on an IBM Z mainframe via a text terminal.
The game uses Wojciech Graj's DOOM-ASCII to replace conventional graphics with colored characters and has no sound.
Gaming sessions are limited to five minutes with support for up to 50 simultaneous users and no installation required.
body: Can an IBM Z mainframe run Doom? Of course it can. The more interesting question is whether you can play it through a text terminal without ruining your eyesight.

WND Software's browser demo connects to an IBM Z mainframe over SSH using its terminal emulator. Wojciech Graj's DOOM-ASCII supplies the text-based carnage, replacing conventional graphics with colored characters. There's no sound.

It is, however, completely playable (although you might need to recalibrate your vision to work out what is going on, particularly with regard to distant objects). Sessions are limited to five minutes, with room for up to 50 simultaneous users, but we had no trouble getting in. ASCII also presented no issues once the game was in motion. This writer played the original shareware release on an Amstrad ALT386SX portable, so squinting at an indistinct demon felt reassuringly familiar.

That Doom can be persuaded to run on an IBM Z mainframe is not particularly noteworthy. The code has turned up everywhere from databases to PCB designers . Even the humble Pi Pico was roped into the fun.

Keeping the action playable through a text terminal is the more entertaining achievement. A year ago, an IBM consultant persuaded Doom to run on IBM Z and LinuxONE using VNC to bring the pixelated mayhem to life. Using a terminal emulator, while a neat demonstration of the capabilities of WND's software, is perhaps more an example of "because I can" masochism.
It's undeniably an enjoyable way to burn through five minutes. No installation or login required – just a willingness to shoot at punctuation. ®

articles.headline: Wendy’s Just Released a Video Game Where You Can Win Fast Food
keyFacts: Wendy’s released a free mobile and desktop role-playing video game called WendyQuest on Nov. 4.
Players aged 18 and older in the US can win codes in the game to redeem for menu items with a purchase.
A Wendy’s spokesperson said WendyQuest is the brand's first fully owned video game after previous gaming culture involvement.
body: Wendy’s has turned its red-headed mascot into a wisecracking warrior who battles evil french fry robots in a free mobile game called WendyQuest. The company announced the retro-style role-playing game on Nov. 4. The announcement came with a promotion where you can win codes in the game, which are redeemable for menu items like fries and burgers at Wendy’s locations.

WendyQuest is available to download on iOS and Android. Desktop users can get it through the Steam platform. Anyone can play the game, but the promotion is restricted to people who are 18 and up living in the US.
You need to sign up for a Wendy’s account to redeem a code. While the food you can win is free, it requires you to buy something when you go.
More from CNET
“Wendy’s has been a part of gaming culture for years, including on Twitch, Fortnite and Feast of Legends, but WendyQuest is the brand’s first fully owned video game,” a spokesperson for Wendy’s said.
Fast-food quest

I downloaded WendyQuest, and my daughter and I played it for a while. The blocky graphics are reminiscent of the home-console video games of the late 1980s and early 1990s. It plays a lot like a simplified version of the DragonQuest, Final Fantasy and Breath of Fire games from the era, only stuffed with fast-food branding.

Rather than the regular turn-based battles that come standard in the early RPGs, this game adds a timing element, where you need to press a button at the right time like you do in old golfing video games.

It’s not a bad game. The light humor is suitable for younger players, and it’s fun to play. Like many RPGs, you battle monsters to gain levels, search around the maps for hidden areas, buy items and talk to people in towns to figure out what’s going on.

It took us over an hour to complete the first region, Fryshire, and get the Fry Stone, which unlocks a promo code for medium fries, free with a purchase. But again, you have to sign up for a Wendy’s account on their website or on the company’s mobile app.
Winning prizes

Video games have a long history of offering real-world prizes to players as promotions. Swordquest, a series of video games released in the early 1980s for the Atari 2600, famously held a contest where players tried to win actual treasure made of gold and jewels.

In 2015, a promotion for the video game Just Cause 3 offered players the chance to win a private island. Developer Square Enix clarified that it couldn’t guarantee that the island would be livable and that the winner would have to pay all the taxes involved.
The reward codes from WendyQuest expire seven days after you get them, and Wendy’s says the codes are first come, first served.
